items.title: Newly Pending Listings Fell 17% In October, The Biggest Year Over Year Drop Since 2023 (Zillow October Market Report)
items.description: Newly Pending Listings Fell 17% In October, The Biggest Year Over Year Drop Since 2023 (Zillow October Market Report) Completed existing home sales fell 9% annually, according to Zillow’s preliminary sales nowcast. Written by Mischa Fisher on November 5, 2026 Key findings: Zillow’s preliminary measure of existing home sales fell 8.7% year over year in October. Newly pending listings — a leading indicator of next month’s closed sales — fell 16.8% year over year, the biggest decrease since August 2023. The typical mortgage payment in October was 12.8% higher than a year ago, according to Zillow’s estimates. The Zillow Observed Rent Index rose 2.9% year over year in October as the rental market continues to strengthen. The acute sting of suddenly higher mortgage rates is having the unfortunate effect on the housing market that last month’s pending sales data foretold. As mortgage rates entrenched themselves above 7%, home sales slowed sharply in October. Existing home sales fell 8.7% year over year, though that largely reflects sales agreed to in September, when mortgage rates were below 7% for much of the month. Newly pending listings, a leading indicator for the next month’s closed sales, fell 16.8% from last October, marking the biggest annual dip since August 2023 and slowest October since 2018. November is shaping up to have an even larger contraction in sales activity, but the silver lining is that next month is likely going to be the worst of it. The pace of the slowdown is expected to ease into the new year. A jump in housing costs likely drove the slowdown. The monthly mortgage payment on the typical U.S. home was an estimated $2,004 in October, assuming a 20% down payment and excluding taxes and insurance. That’s up 12.8% from last year and 4.8% higher than in September, the biggest one-month jump in four years. For a buyer putting only 5% down and securing an FHA loan, which comes with a lower mortgage rate, the year-over-year rise has been similar at 11.8%. Once insurance, taxes and maintenance are factored in, a median-income household would spend 41.5% of its income on that monthly payment, up from 39.2% a year ago. The rise in mortgage costs is almost exclusively due to higher mortgage rates. The typical U.S. home value fell 0.6% month over month and is just 0.7% higher than a year earlier, as measured by the Zillow Home Value Index. Meanwhile, mortgage rates averaged 7.33% in October, according to Freddie Mac , up from 6.86% in September. As for-sale activity wanes, the rental market continues to strengthen. The typical U.S. rent is up 2.9% year over year, according to the Zillow Observed Rent Index. That’s the strongest annual gain in the past 19 months, and marks the seventh consecutive month that annual rent growth has increased. While there is no avoiding that this has been a very soft fall for for-sale activity, there are deals to be had for buyers able to brave the affordability headwinds in the coming months. Buyers usually have leverage this time of year when sellers try to make a deal before the holidays, and especially so this year given current market conditions. The continued inventory buildup means there is a lot of upside for sales into next year if we get rate relief. More data, including dashboards with local market data , can be found on the refreshed Zillow Research website . The Zillow November Market Report is expected to be released December 4 . Home Values & Mortgage Payments The typical U.S. home value is $364,812, according to the Zillow Home Value Index (ZHVI). ZHVI fell 0.6% month over month in October. Home values are 0.7% higher than a year earlier. The monthly mortgage payment on a typical U.S. home is $2,004, assuming a 20% down payment and excluding taxes and insurance. That is 12.8% higher than last year. Inventory There were 1.4 million homes for sale nationwide in October. Active inventory was 3.4% higher than a year earlier. Inventory rose 0.4% from September. New for-sale listings totaled 328,328 in October, down 4.2% from a year earlier and down 4.4% from September. Sales 304,105 homes were sold in October, according to the preliminary Zillow sales count nowcast. That is 8.7% lower than a year earlier and down 5.4% from September. These figures will be revised mid-month. Newly pending listings, which measures listings that changed from for-sale to pending status rather than closed sales, shows a 16.8% decrease from a year earlier and a 9.1% decrease over September. Affordability A household earning the median income would need to spend 34.7% of its income on the typical monthly mortgage payment (assuming a typically valued home and a 20% down payment, and including estimates for taxes, maintenance and insurance). That is up from 32.7% a year earlier and up from 33.5% in September. A household earning the median income would need to spend 26% of its income on the typical rent in October. That is unchanged from a year earlier and from September. Competition Homes took a median of 31 days to go pending in October. That was two days longer than a year earlier and two days longer than September. The share of listings with a price cut in October was 26.5%. That was down from 26.9% a year earlier and down from 27.3% in September. 25.6% of homes sold above list price in September, the most recent data available. That’s compared to 25.2% a year earlier and 27.5% in August. Rents The typical rent nationwide is $1,913, according to the Zillow Observed Rent Index. That’s 2.9% higher than a year earlier and flat from September. 40.4% of rental listings on Zillow offered a concession in October. That’s up from 38.7% a year earlier and up from 39.6% in September. items.title: October 2026 Jobs Report: Employment growth tops market forecasts
items.description: October 2026 Jobs Report: Employment growth tops market forecasts Written by Kenny Lee on November 6, 2026 Key findings U.S. employers added 165,000 jobs in October, while gains in September and August were revised up by a combined 84,000. The unemployment rate slipped to 4.1% from 4.2% as strong employment growth absorbed an increase in labor force participation. Wage growth continued to cool compared to recent years, with average hourly earnings rising 3.1% year over year. What happened: The nonfarm payroll employment rose 165,000 in October, topping financial market expectations. Combined with strong upward revisions to increases in September and August, the Bureau of Labor Statistics report this month indicates a meaningful improvement in job growth. The increases in employment were broad-based across key industries such as professional and business services (+70,000); healthcare and social assistance (+55,000); and transportation and warehousing (+25,000). Employment in temporary help services, a leading indicator for overall labor demand, soared to 18,600. The household survey also indicates a resilient labor market. The labor force participation rate increased to 61.9% from 61.8% as more workers rejoined the workforce. Combined with strong increases in employment, the unemployment rate fell to 4.1% from 4.2%. Why it matters for housing: Stable employment and wage growth give households the confidence to buy a home or sign a new lease, but the housing market is already feeling the chilling effects of the recent surge in mortgage rates. Zillow data points to a colder-than-usual fall market: our preliminary measure of existing home sales fell 8.7% year over year in October. Newly pending listings — a leading indicator of next month’s closed sales — fell 16.8% year over year, the biggest decrease since August 2023. With mortgage rates above 7%, affordability headwinds in the housing market may still feel insurmountable — even for those who have a job or recently found one. This is consistent with our expectation for a more substantial decline in existing home sales and slower growth in home value in Q4. While mortgage rates have been declining from their recent peak, it is difficult to know how far they will fall when forces pushing up Treasury yields, such as anxiety over government deficits and geopolitical impact on energy prices, remain at play. But when mortgage rates come down, eventually, buyers will be ready. The Bureau of Labor Statistics report today is consistent with a stable labor market in a growing economy. The resilient labor market will pave the way for a housing market thaw. items.title: Mortgage Rates Drift Lower, but Spring Shopping Season Might Still See Rates Above 7%
items.description: Mortgage Rates Drift Lower, but Spring Shopping Season Might Still See Rates Above 7% Zillow expects mortgage rates to remain above 7% for the rest of 2026 through mid-2027, presenting a possible headwind for next year’s home shopping season. Written by Kara Ng on November 4, 2026 In short: Mortgage rates are easing from their recent peak, but Zillow expects them to stay above 7% through mid-2027 — likely leading to a chillier 2027 spring home shopping season. Mortgage rates continue to retreat Mortgage rates continue their decline from the recent peak, though they remain challenging for housing affordability. As of November 4, oil prices fell on hopes of easing geopolitical tensions and markets are weighing the potential effects of restrictions on data center construction. Whether the forces keeping bond yields elevated — government deficits, geopolitical impacts on prices, and corporate borrowing to fund AI spending — could sustainably fade remains an open question. Zillow expects mortgage rates to remain above 7% for the rest of 2026 through mid-2027, presenting a possible headwind for next year’s home shopping season. What’s the impact on housing? Challenging affordability continues to weigh on the for-sale market. Newly pending sales, a leading indicator of future closings, fell 17% in October , the biggest year over year drop since 2023. At the same time, rental demand skyrocketed, with rental engagement per listing (as measured by ZORDI ) growing 22% in October compared to last year, as elevated borrowing costs push would-be buyers to rent instead. With little relief in the mortgage rate outlook, the spring 2027 home shopping season could arrive with rates still above 7%, which may hamper activity. items.title: MORE HOUSTON HOUSEHOLDS ABLE TO AFFORD A HOME AS PRICES EASE
items.description: MORE HOUSTON HOUSEHOLDS ABLE TO AFFORD A HOME AS PRICES EASE 42% of Houston-area households were able to buy a home in the third quarter HOUSTON -- (November 5, 2026) -- More Houston-area households were able to buy a home in the third quarter as home prices eased, according to the latest Housing and Rental Affordability Report from the Houston Association of Realtors. HAR's Housing Affordability Index shows that 42% of households in the Greater Houston area could afford a median-priced home, up from 39% in the third quarter of 2025. The median home price declined 0.4% year over year to $340,300 from $341,600 the prior year. The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate was 6.68%, compared with 6.57% during the same quarter last year. The typical monthly mortgage payment, including principal, taxes and insurance, was $2,520, compared with $2,510 in Q3 2025. Households needed a minimum annual income of $100,800 to purchase the median-priced home, which is flat from a year earlier. "Affordability is moving in the right direction, and that's encouraging, but we also know many consumers are still concerned about the cost of buying a home, particularly with mortgage rates remaining elevated," said HAR Chair Theresa Hill with Compass RE Texas, LLC -- Houston. "For buyers who may have been sitting on the sidelines, it's worth taking another look at what's possible. A Realtor can help buyers understand their options and determine what's realistic for their budget." Across Texas, 45% of households could afford a median-priced home in the third quarter, compared with 42% last year. The statewide median home price declined to $335,000 from $337,500, while the minimum annual income needed to purchase the median-priced home held at $92,400. Nationally, 38% of households could afford a median-priced home, up from 35% in 2025. According to the National Association of Realtors, the U.S. median home price increased to $432,900 from $426,800. The minimum qualifying income rose to $112,000 from $109,200. The chart below shows how the minimum annual household income needed to purchase a home has changed year-over-year. Rental Affordability Update Forty-four percent of Houston-area households could afford the median monthly lease payment in the third quarter of 2026, according to HAR's Rental Affordability Index. That is down from 45% in 2025. The median monthly lease was $2,195 compared with $2,200 a year earlier. A household needed a minimum annual income of $87,800 to qualify for the median lease payment, compared with $88,000 the prior year. The chart below shows how the median lease price for a single-family home has changed year-over-year. Highlights of the Q3 2026 Housing & Rental Affordability Report: • 42% of Greater Houston households could afford a median-priced home, up from 39% in Q3 2025. • The median home price declined 0.4% to $340,300 from $341,600 in Q3 2025. • The monthly mortgage payment was $2,520, compared with $2,510 in Q3 2025. • The minimum annual income needed to purchase a median-priced home was $100,800, compared with $100,400 in Q3 2025. • 44% of Houston-area households could afford the average lease payment on a single-family rental home, compared to 45% a year earlier. • The median lease price in the Houston area decreased slightly to $2,195. And the election results could shape the federal housing agenda, plus local zoning and property taxes in several states. But whoever wins on Tuesday, come Wednesday morning, all of those political ads will finally be over. And that’s something we’ll all be happy about. I’m Jake Krimmel, senior economist at Realtor.com, sitting in for chief economist Danielle Hale . Let’s get into the Weekly Housing Outlook . Featured Report This week’s featured report is a two-for-one. Each quarter, we partner with The Wall Street Journal to find the top-ranked housing markets in America, covering the overall market and the luxury tier. Since summer, a lot has changed. Mortgage rates climbed from around 6.4% in July to over 7% by the end of September. Let’s see how those tougher conditions shaped the rankings. Senior economist Hannah Jones ranked the 200 largest metros on housing market conditions, local economies, and livability. Whenever mortgage rates climb, we start talking about refuge markets again. Those are places where each dollar goes further, so buyers head there when affordability takes a hit. And this quarter’s top-10 list is basically a map of refuge markets. Half are in the Great Lakes states, including Appleton, Wisconsin, South Bend, Indiana and Canton, OH. What a season for Wisconsin by the way. The Brewers win the World Series and Appleton takes the number one spot. The other half of the top 10 are smaller metros near pricier ones, like Lancaster and Reading outside of Philadelphia, or Manchester, New Hampshire, a short drive from Boston. These markets are all about relative bargains. In Canton, Ohio, for example, the typical monthly payment runs a third below the national average. But people will pay for value, and the secret is getting out. Asking prices across the top-20 are up 1.1% over the past year, while prices nationally are down. Senior economist Anthony Smith ran the same exercise for 60 luxury markets , and those buyers are chasing value too. Lifestyle markets that led earlier this year, like Boulder and San Jose, fell out of the top 10 in the fall. And St. Louis meanwhile grabbed the headlines, jumping from number 12 to number 1. Luxury starts around $670,000 there, versus $1.2 million nationally. So a national luxury budget would land you in the top 5% of St. Louis listings. Two metros made both the overall and luxury lists: Portland, Maine, and Bridgeport, Connecticut. I guess everyone really does love New England in the fall. The Week Ahead: Now, to the week ahead. Wednesday brings our October monthly housing trends report, written by yours truly. I’ll take a look at whether elevated mortgage rates caused buyers or sellers to pull back more, as well as what happened to inventory, asking prices, and contract signings. As we await October’s data, let’s take a look back at the September snapshot, which showed a housing market softening under the weight of rising mortgage rates. Median list prices fell, while inventory and price cuts rose. I expect more of the same from the October data, when mortgage rates hit their highest levels since 2023. Speaking of mortgage rates, Thursday brings another Freddie Mac reading and commentary from senior economist Hannah Jones , alongside the Realtor.com weekly data update. It’s too early to call the direction of rates this week. But I’ll be watching the bond market, especially the 10-year yield, for any reaction to the midterms, new developments in the Middle East, and any Fed signals about a December hike. items.title: Mortgage Rates Fall for a Third Straight Week
items.description: Mortgage Rates Fall for a Third Straight Week By Hannah Jones Nov 05, 2026 What happened to mortgage rates this week? The Freddie Mac 30-year fixed mortgage rate fell 6 basis points to 7.18% this week as bond yields eased. That marks a third straight week of declines, though rates remain about one percentage point above year-ago levels. Markets were focused on the midterm elections and incoming jobs data, both of which shape expectations for future policy. Tuesday’s Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey came in stronger than expected, with layoffs down slightly and a significant gain in job openings. That points to a potentially strong jobs report on Friday. While solid hiring supports housing demand over time, a stronger-than-expected report could also lift bond yields and slow the pace of rate declines in the near term. Tuesday’s midterm elections gave Democrats a majority in both the House and Senate, as winning candidates connected with voters’ dissatisfaction with the economy. It is not yet clear whether the shift will be felt in the housing market. Many newly elected representatives have voiced discontent with the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, which has contributed to rising inflation, so any progress toward resolution could mean lower inflation and softer mortgage rates ahead. What does this mean for the housing market? Although rates have eased over the last few weeks, they remain above 7%, keeping many buyers on the sidelines. October marked another month of a slowing housing market , with both buyers and sellers pulling back. Pending sales fell 10.5% year over year, the steepest decline in three years, as buyers contend with diminished purchasing power. New listings fell 7.5% year over year as sellers held back, discouraged by weak demand. Still, sellers aren’t delisting in droves, which suggests they are disengaging rather than acting out of distress. With 43% of active listings having had a price reduction, buyers who can afford to participate are in a relatively strong position, facing less competition and more price cuts.

items.title: Weekly Housing Trends: U.S. Market Update (Week Ending Oct. 31, 2026)
items.description: Weekly Housing Trends: U.S. Market Update (Week Ending Oct. 31, 2026) By Joel Berner Nov 05, 2026 Welcome to this weekly housing trends update, where we bring you the latest snapshot of inventory trends, listing activity, and buyer-seller dynamics across the U.S. housing market. In addition to our monthly housing trends reports , which offer deeper insights into long-term patterns, we publish these weekly updates to provide more timely views into market changes. This effort began in response to rapid shifts in the economy and housing landscape. You can count on a new Weekly Housing Trends update, fresh weekly data each Thursday, and a weekly video from our economists to help you stay informed. What this week’s data shows Mortgage rates above 7% have once again been a major drag on the housing market this week. Buyers are seeing their purchasing power diminish, and many are simply opting out of buying homes altogether. Many sellers are opting out as well, with the knowledge that finding a buyer who will offer a desirable price is getting harder and harder. We’re seeing prices falling, fewer sellers listing, and homes spending longer on the market as the market seems to be entering its winter freeze early. For buyers who can manage to avoid financing their home purchase with a mortgage, though, opportunities for great deals abound. Our October data show the inventory of homes for sale at its closest level to pre-pandemic norms yet, and price reductions are even higher than they were last year at this time. The best time to buy a home has passed at the national level, but several markets still have their prime opportunities upcoming. Active inventory climbed 8.8% year-over-year The number of homes for sale rose 8.8% compared to a year ago, the highest weekly growth rate since late January. Inventory has been building momentum throughout the fall, rising from roughly 4% year-over-year growth in late August to nearly 9% now. The pickup is not being driven by a flood of new sellers. Instead, the slowdown in buyer activity is allowing unsold listings to accumulate, pushing the overall count higher. Year-to-date, active inventory i s up 4.9%. Homes spent 1 day longer on the market compared to a year ago Median days on market came in at 65 days, with homes selling one day slower than the same time last year. This marks the second week in a row that time on market has slowed after a long stretch reaching back to May of homes selling faster than last year. As mortgage rates top 7%, more buyers are retreating to the sidelines, and the shift could be an early signal of market slowdown. Year-to-date, time on market remains 2 days behind last year’s pace. New listings, a measure of sellers putting homes up for sale, fell 5.2% year-over-year New listing activity took a sharp turn downward this week, dropping 5.2% year over year. Sellers are discouraged because buyers are discouraged. The prices the market will bear are less appealing to sellers than they were when mortgage rates were lower, and the difference between current rates and the rates many would-be sellers are sitting on in their has grown, making relocating a less attractive proposition. The stronger new listing activity earlier in the year has the year-to-date change at -0.4%. The median listing price fell 2.1% year-over-year The median listing price dropped to $410,000, down 2.1% from the same week last year. Listing prices have now been negative on a year-over-year basis for 42 consecutive weeks. The median price per square foot also declined, falling 1.4% year over year. Mortgage rates have buyers in an affordability crunch that has diminished their willingness to pay, and the median price in the market is slowly responding. Year-to-date, median listing prices sit 1.9% below 2025 levels.

Economy In third quarter 2026, the Reno area recorded 287,200 jobs, with unemployment declining 20 basis points (bps) year-over-year (YOY) to 4.0%. The region continued to exhibit steady growth, with households increasing 1.7% YOY to 239,300. Wage growth remained a key driver of labor force expansion, as median household income reached $95,300, up 3.9% YOY. Supply & Demand The Reno multifamily market continued to tighten in third quarter 2026, with overall vacancy declining 230 bps YOY and 10 bps quarter-over-quarter (QOQ) to 5.5%, the lowest level since 2022. Improved occupancy was driven by continued tenant demand, as the market recorded 166 units of net absorption during the quarter and 898 units year-to-date (YTD), extending Reno's streak of positive net absorption to 17 consecutive quarters. The University submarket led both quarterly and YTD net absorption with gains of 61 units and 222 units, respectively, while South Reno added 31 units during the quarter and 176 units YTD. In contrast, Carson City County was the only submarket to post negative net absorption in the third quarter, recording a loss of eight units. Limited new supply further supported market fundamentals, with just 96 units completed during both the quarter and YTD, well below the 10-year average of 1,344 annual construction completions. Construction activity remains modest with only 698 units underway, including Village at Cross Creek in Carson City County and Argent Flats in South Reno. Tight conditions in several submarkets continued to constrain available inventory, particularly in areas near major employment centers and newer housing stock. As demand continues to outpace construction completions and the development pipeline remains limited, the market is well positioned for continued occupancy gains through the remainder of 2026. Pricing Average monthly asking rents increased 5.9% YOY to $1,813 per unit, while effective rents rose 7.1% YOY to $1,776 per unit. Rent growth remained broad-based across the market, with South Reno and Sparks/Spanish Springs posting the highest effective annual rent growth at 9.3%, followed by West Reno at 7.2% and the University submarket at 7.1%. South Reno continued to command the region's highest effective rent at $2,045 per unit, reflecting strong demand for newer product and amenity-rich communities. As vacancy continues to decline and development activity remains limited, rental rates are expected to maintain positive momentum through 2027. items.title: US home price insights — November 2026
items.description: Overview: Home prices continue to rise nationally, up 1.7%, but momentum is moderating with a 0.3% monthly decline, and annual growth forecasted to slow to 0.9%. Compared with August, appreciation strengthened in about half of metros and weakened in the other half, suggesting no single national trajectory. Annual appreciation was led by northeastern and Great Lakes states, paced by Illinois (6.9%), Rhode Island (6.4%), Connecticut (6.0%), New Jersey (5.1%), and Ohio (4.9%). National home price growth September 2026 data Source: Cotality ‍ Affordability meter Source: Cotality ‍ ‍ Market activity will favor regions with solid economic prospects, regions that attract retiring population and offer affordable homes. Dr. Selma Hepp Cotality Chief Economist Insights from Chief Economist Dr. Selma Hepp As autumn arrived, the U.S. housing market cooled further. In September 2026, single-family home prices rose just 1.7% year-over-year and dropped 0.3% from August, pushing the national median above $400,000. This was the largest monthly decline since 2022 and the third consecutive September without growth, as high mortgage rates curbed summer demand. Normally, home prices edge up about 0.2% in September. But national averages still hide a key divide: Every Northeast and Midwest state saw annual price gains, while four Western and two Southern states posted declines. The market is nearly evenly split between areas accelerating and those slowing. Many Northeastern and Midwestern markets have gained 25% to 30% since mid-2022, while much of the West and Texas have seen little or no net growth. This regional divide sharpened considerably heading into the final stretch of the year. Chronic inventory shortages in the Great Lakes and New England fueled strong annual gains— Illinois (6.9%), Rhode Island (6.4%), Connecticut (6.0%), New Jersey (5.1%), and Ohio (4.9%). Meanwhile, prices dropped in former boom states: Washington (-1.0%), Wyoming (-0.7%), Texas (-0.4%), Hawaii (-0.1%), and Utah (-0.0%). Since June 2022, Rhode Island, Connecticut, and New Jersey have surged 30–31%, while Washington, Colorado, and Texas are up less than 1%, and D.C. is down 2%. “Potential homebuyers are feeling the pinch from rising costs across the board, especially for daily living expenses,” said Cotality Chief Economist Dr. Selma Hepp. “Meanwhile, limited job opportunities and slow wage growth are making households reluctant to move.” Leading metros for recent price growth include Cleveland, Albany, Providence, Greensboro, and St. Louis—places marked by affordability, job growth, in-migration, and recent price resets. In contrast, the fastest-cooling markets, like Augusta, Austin, Seattle, San Jose, and Washington, DC, have seen job losses, higher inventory, and declining affordability. Rising mortgage rates have sharply reduced affordability. When the 30-year fixed rate rose from 6.5% to 7.5%, the monthly payment on a median-priced home jumped $300, pushing the required annual income to $103,000. In California, buyers need $180,900 for a $754,500 median home. In Florida and Texas ($369,750 median), higher insurance and taxes often push total costs above borrowing limits, fueling declines in metros like Austin (-2.0%) and Dallas (-1.0%). “Elevated mortgage rates are expected to limit home buying opportunities in 2027,” concluded Dr. Hepp. “However, more inventory and greater buyer bargaining power will keep home price growth subdued, improving affordability. Market activity will favor regions with solid economic prospects, regions that attract retiring population and offer affordable homes.” -Dr. Selma Hepp Cotality’s Chief Economist Dive deeper Home price indexes Top 10 hottest markets Source: Cotality ‍ Top 10 coolest markets Source: Cotality ‍ Which areas are affordable? items.title: Mortgage rates fell and demand steadied as inventory dipped
items.description: Mortgage rates fell, demand stabilized and inventory had a noticeable decline last week. But are the changes in demand and inventory data about seasonality, or has the housing market changed with the recent mortgage rate decline? Let’s take a look at the weekend tracker and see what the data is telling us with rates falling the last three weeks. 10-year yield and mortgage rates In the 2026 HousingWire forecast , I anticipated the following ranges: Mortgage rates between 5.75% and 6.75% The 10-year yield fluctuating between 3.80% and 4.60% What a crazy time in the bond market recently: the key level of 5.35% has not only held since early October, but the reversal has been truly nice to watch. The midterm elections , which changed the control of the House and Senate, have added another variable into the mortgage rate equation. I discussed what Congress can do to help lower mortgage rates on this episode of the HousingWire Daily podcast with Editor in Chief Sarah Wheeler, but for now the head-and-shoulders pattern of the 10-year yield is still somewhat intact, though a fight for it to break lower is happening. I wouldn’t get too excited about mortgage rates until the 10-year yield can break under 4.70% and have follow-through bond buying, but mortgage rates have fallen and demand has stabilized over the last few weeks. Mortgage spreads Mortgage spreads have worsened recently, but they’re still trending near multiyear lows. Traditionally, when mortgage rates escalate with the 10-year yield and then make a big reversal — like we just had from a 5.35% 10-year yield top that dropped down toward 4.82% — spreads do get worse to try to compress mortgage rate volatility. That said, if mortgage spreads weren’t near multiyear lows right now, we'd have no chance of getting mortgage rates below 7.25%, and demand wouldn't have stabilized recently. Now that spreads have moved up from this year's lows, we can clearly see that mortgage rates would be sub-7% if spreads return to that level. Historically, mortgage spreads have ranged from 1.60% to 1.80%. Last week, spreads rose to 2.27% from 2.23% a week earlier. Let’s compare last week’s mortgage rates to where they would have been at the best spread levels this year and the worst levels of this cycle. If we had the best levels of spreads in 2026, mortgage rates would be 6.72% today, not 7.17% . If we had the worst mortgage spread levels of 2023, mortgage rates would be 8.11% today, not 7.17% . Weekly pending sales Our pending home sales data provides a week-to-week perspective, though holidays and short-term fluctuations can affect results. This weekly pending sales data typically takes 30-60 days to reflect in sales data. The key for the last three weeks: lower rates, even above 7%, have stabilized demand, as our weekly pending sales have shown. Now, this isn’t growth, just stabilization from a noticeable slowdown when mortgage rates got toward 7.60%. The last three years and 10 months show that housing demand grows when mortgage rates fall below 6.64% and head toward 6%; above 7%, we don’t have much growth data beyond seasonal demand. Last year at this time, mortgage rates were headed toward 6%, so the year-over-year comps will be hard for some time. Here are the pending sales for last week over the last two years: 2026: 51,764 2025: 59,164 Purchase applications Purchase application data, which looks out 30-90 days, has softened as mortgage rates rose above 6.64% and are now above 7%. We had a small decline week to week; I can see the stabilization here as well and the year-over-year comps will also be very difficult here, as last year at this time rates were heading toward 6%. Earlier in the year, when rates were lower, pretty much every week this year showed growth. Here are the stats on purchase apps so far in 2026: 16 positive week-to-week prints 24 negative week-to-week prints 5 flat week-to-week prints 10 weeks of double-digit year-over-year growth 25 weeks of positive year-over-year growth 15 negative year-over-year prints Housing inventory Housing inventory growth has been very tame this year, with some weeks being down year over year. However, when mortgage rates got above 6.64% and then headed toward 7.60%, we did see some growth pick up. Also, rates were lower last year so demand was heading toward a nine-month high in December, which means it the comps will be easier to show growth in inventory. Inventory growth is running at 7.18% even with easier comps. Weekly inventory change (Oct. 30-Nov. 6): Inventory fell from 914,833 to 902,740 Same week last year (Oct. 31-Nov 7): Inventory fell from 856,751 to 842,257 New listings New listings are in their typical seasonal decline; 2026 has been the healthiest new-listings year since 2022, with over 80,000 new listings per week a few times this year. The concern I had was that if higher rates cause sellers to stop listing their homes — as they did in the second half of 2022 — that would hurt supply and demand. However, that hasn’t happened in any meaningful way. Most home sellers are buyers, and now that rates have fallen a smidge, it looks like we can end the year on a positive note for 2026 for new listings. In a normal environment, new listings range from 80,000 to 100,000 per week during peak periods. For context, during the housing bubble years, new listings ranged from 250,000 to 400,000 per week for several years . Here is last week’s new listings data for the past two years: 2026: 54,479 2025: 55,486 Price-cut percentage Typically, about one-third of homes see price reductions before they sell, reflecting the housing market’s dynamic nature. Overall, price-cut percentages this year have been lower than last year. This held true until rates moved above 6.64% and then above 7%; demand fell, and the year-over-year price-cut percentage rose 1%. items.title: Annual rent growth sees a milestone, even as prices ease in October
items.description: Annual rent growth sees a milestone, even as prices ease in October by Kim O'Brien Posted November 6, 2026 in Market Research October marked the first month of rent cuts in the U.S. apartment market in 2026, but annual gains continue at a robust pace. Same-store effective asking rents increased 1.7% year-over-year, according to October data from RealPage Market Analytics . That was the market’s biggest annual price increase since May 2023. While the annual reading has improved, the gain stemmed less from robust monthly pricing and more from weak rent performance falling out of the annual calculation. In fact, rents came down a mild 0.7% during October, marking the first monthly rent cut in the U.S. in calendar 2026. U.S. apartment occupancy faded to 95% in October, easing 20 basis points (bps) from the September showing. Still, October occupancy is up 40 bps in the calendar year and remains 10 bps ahead of the October 2025 showing. Helping support occupancy and rent performance, the U.S. apartment market has seen supply and demand edge closer to balance recently. Renters absorbed nearly 304,800 conventional apartments in the year-ending 3rd quarter 2026, gaining ground on a cooling supply wave. Developers completed nearly 318,000 units in the past year, nearly half the recent peak from late 2024. Bay Area and Midwest markets still lead for rent growth Rent performance remained sharply split by market. Coastal tech hubs and Midwest metros delivered the strongest annual gains, while most Sun Belt markets kept logging rent declines. Northern California's tech-driven markets posted the three strongest gains among the 50 largest apartment markets in the year-ending October. San Francisco saw rents hike 14.7% over the past year, San Jose followed at 9.5%, and Oakland reached 8.5%. All three markets are running near 97% occupancy. Midwest markets make up much of the rest of the top 10 list. Milwaukee led the major Midwest markets with annual rent growth of 4.2%, followed by Chicago (3.3%), Kansas City (3.1%) and Cleveland (3.1%). Detroit and St. Louis both fell just shy of making the cut, with annual rent growth of 2.7% in each market. Sun Belt rents still trail, but the gap is narrowing The South region overall has returned to annual rent growth, though barely, at 0.5% in October. Sun Belt and Florida markets continue to see the nation’s steepest declines. San Antonio had the deepest cut among big markets at 2.6%, stemming from occupancy at 92.5%, also dead last among the largest 50 markets. Also posting rent declines in the year-ending October were Houston (-1.8%), Tampa (-1%), Charlotte (-0.9%) and Denver (-0.8%). The bigger story, however, is how many Sun Belt markets have stopped seeing rent positioning hemorrhage. Annual increases have returned to Phoenix (0.4%) and Austin (0.6%), as well as Atlanta (0.8%), Raleigh (1.0%), Miami (0.6%) and Jacksonville (2.6%). Compare Historical PMMS Results Frequently Asked Questions Toggle all accordion sections Expand All What data is used for PMMS? The PMMS results are based on data from our Loan Product Advisor (LPA): mortgage rates collected from thousands of loan applications submitted to Freddie Mac from lenders across the country when a borrower applies for a mortgage. For more detailed information, see Enhanced Mortgage Rate Survey Explained . How is the national average determined? We collect the mortgage rate of all purchase applications based on PMMS criteria and a national average mortgage rate is calculated out of all the selected loan applications. The criteria include weekly conventional, single-family originations with conforming loan limits as set by FHFA. Is the PMMS rate based on current lender quotes or recent settlements? PMMS rates are based on applications submitted to Freddie Mac for the given week from lenders across the country. What type of lenders are included in the PMMS? Currently, our lenders are a mix of credit unions, commercial banks and mortgage lending companies. Do the PMMS results represent the rates charged on a specific day of the week? If so, which day? Or are they the average rate charged that week? PMMS is published each Thursday at noon ET. When a U.S. holiday falls on a Thursday, the PMMS will publish on the Wednesday of that week. The week of application activity starts at 12:00 a.m. ET the prior Thursday and lasts through 11:59 p.m. ET Wednesday. Therefore, the PMMS results are an average of loan rates offered Thursday through Wednesday. See our publication calendar . Why are adjustable rates no longer published? ARMs indexed to alternatives to U.S. Treasury securities have become more prevalent in the market. As we worked on enhancing the PMMS , we carefully considered which loan products were most popular for the PMMS borrower profile (good/excellent credit, 20% loans, home purchase loans on owner occupied 1-unit single-family properties). Additionally, in recent years the mortgage market has been dominated by fixed mortgage products. While there has been an uptick recently in the share of adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs) for the broader mortgage market, ARMs remain most popular for higher loan size (nonconforming) loans. Why are fees/points no longer published? Under the current LPA requirements, fees and points are not always required to be provided by lenders. Therefore, we are not able to report on the average fees and points. How has PMMS changed over time? Since April 1971, Freddie Mac shared the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rate with the PMMS. We have updated the information we collect and the process for gathering data over time. Changes in Data Processes When it was launched, PMMS surveyed lenders on the rates and points for their most popular 30-year fixed-rate, 15-year fixed-rate and 5/1 hybrid amortizing adjustable-rate mortgage products. The survey was based on first-lien prime conventional conforming home purchase mortgages with a loan-to-value of 80 percent. In addition, the adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) products were indexed to U.S. Treasury yields, and lenders were asked for both the initial coupon rate and points as well as the margin on the ARM products. Lenders surveyed each week were a mix of lender types — credit unions, commercial banks and mortgage lending companies — roughly proportional to the level of mortgage business that each type commands nationwide. On November 17, 2022, the mortgage rate gathering process was updated. Instead of surveying lenders, we now use data from our Loan Product Advisor (LPA). Changes in Information Shared In 1984 , the 1-year ARM was added to the survey. In 1991 , the 15-year fixed-rate mortgage rate was added. In January 2005 , a 5/1 hybrid ARM series was added. In January 2016 , the 1-year ARM was discontinued. In November 2022 , adjustable rates and fees/points were discontinued. For more detailed information, see Enhanced Mortgage Rate Survey Explained . items.title: Mortgage Rates Climb in October Amid Accelerating Inflation
items.description: Mortgage Rates Climb in October Amid Accelerating Inflation November 3, 2026 Catherine Koh No Comments Mortgage rates rose sharply again in October as the U.S. treasury yields surged. According to Freddie Mac , the 30-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 7.33% in October, up 47 basis points (bps) from September. The rate reached 7.40% in early October, its highest level since 2023, before easing toward the end of the month. Since the conflict in the Middle East began, the 30-year mortgage rate has increased by approximately 128 bps. The 15-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 6.66% in October, up 46 bps from September and 123 bps from the end of February. Compared with a year ago, the average 30-year and 15-year mortgage rates were higher by 108 bps and 117 bps, respectively. The 10-year Treasury yield, a key benchmark for long-term borrowing, increased 21 bps to an average of 5.15% in October, although yields eased during the latter part of the month. Inflation concerns continued to put upward pressure on Treasury yields, as elevated energy prices stemming from the ongoing conflict with Iran contributed to accelerating inflation. Inflation accelerated to 3.7% in September from 3.4% in August. Energy prices were a major contributor, with fuel oil prices rising 15.3% and gasoline prices increasing 9.1% over the month. At its latest meeting, the Federal Reserve held the federal funds rate unchanged at 3.75% to 4.00%. However, there were two dissenters who voted for a 25 bps increase. The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) described economic activity as expanding at a “strong pace,” an improvement from the “solid pace” noted in September. The committee pointed to resilient consumer spending and strong business investment as signs of continued economic strength, while noting that inflation remained elevated and uncertainty persisted. items.title: Camden lowers guidance after September concession resurgence
items.description: Camden lowers guidance after September concession resurgence The REIT still saw improvement in expenses and new lease growth in Q3, though rising interest rates forced it to cancel property and land acquisitions. Published Nov. 6, 2026 Leslie Shaver Senior Reporter Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google Wall Street sign with american flags and New York Stock Exchange in Manhattan, New York City, USA. Getty Images Camden’s Property Trust lowered its 2026 same-store revenue midpoint by 50 basis points to 0% after a weaker-than-expected September and the expectation of greater seasonal decline in the fourth quarter, according to the REIT’s executives on Friday’s third-quarter earnings call. Performance in September, specifically, surprised the company and set the stage for that revision, according to CEO Alex Jessett. “It was a greater decline in traffic than we had expected,” Jessett said. “And when we had the decline in traffic, obviously, you have to reduce your prices if you're trying to increase traffic.” Jessett said concessions, which were “incredibly sticky,” ranged from three weeks in West Palm Beach, Florida, up to two months in Austin, Texas, as merchant builders continued to offer steep discounts. “The third quarter, at least July and August, were so strong that we would have expected to see others start to dial back their concessions, and they absolutely did not do it,” Jessett said. Despite the September slowdown, there were positives: Camden expects same-store YOY expense growth of 1.75%, which is 75 bps better than the REIT’s prior midpoint and 125 bps better than beginning-of-year guidance, according to CFO Ben Fraker. The company was also “the only S&P 500 multifamily REIT to experience sequential improvement for both new lease rates and blended lease rates each quarter this year, and we were the only one with second- to third-quarter acceleration,” according to Jessett. Camden saw positive signs into Q4, though high-concession markets weighed on results. The REIT finalized its massive California sale and multiple acquisitions, though the interest rate environment forced it to cancel other deals. Rent trends Like many companies in supply heavy markets, Camden saw new leases remain in negative territory in Q3, falling to -2% YOY, according to its Q3 earnings release. In Q2, Camden’s new lease rate came in 130 bps lower at -3.3%. In Q3, renewals rose 3.6% YOY, giving the REIT a blended rate of 1%. In Q2, renewals increased 2.8% YOY and blends were -0.2%. “While renewal growth was in line with our expectations, new lease and blended lease growth were at the low end of our anticipated ranges, likely driven by the persistent concessions that remain in many of our core markets and sub-markets,” Camden Chief Operating Officer Laurie Baker said on the Q3 call. Camden sent out renewal offers to residents with December and January expirations at an average increase of 4.5%, according to Baker. That isn’t the only positive indicator. “We have seen signed new leases improve pretty dramatically in October as compared to September, and when we look at our October numbers and we compare them to October of last year, we're seeing really significant improvement,” Jessett said. Southeast Florida, at 1.6% YOY revenue growth; Atlanta, at 1.5%; Dallas, at 0.8%; and Houston, at 0.6%, were the top markets for Camden in Q3, according to a company Securities & Exchange Commission filing. Concessions have played a role in their performance, according to Baker. “We're seeing the strongest markets in Atlanta, Southeast Florida, Dallas and Houston,” Baker said. “And so, where those lower concessions are, we're obviously getting a little more pricing power, and we're having the ability to improve our occupancy.” On the other end of the spectrum were Denver, with a 5% YOY revenue decline; Nashville at -3.1%; Tampa, Florida, at -1.3%; and Orlando, Florida, at -0.7%, according to the SEC filing. “We still are continuing to see Denver and Nashville as those that have concessions that have been persistent,” Baker said. Buying and selling In July, Camden closed its sale of 11 properties with 3,620 apartment homes to a BlackRock-managed vehicle for $1.6 billion, recognizing a gain of $1 billion. The REIT used approximately $0.9 billion to retire balances outstanding under its unsecured revolving credit facility and commercial paper program, according to the Q3 earnings release. The REIT used $125 million to fund its August property and land acquisitions; $50 million to repurchase shares in August and early September; and $495 million toward the redemption of $500 million of senior notes due in November and to pay down borrowings in its commercial paper program. It had $55 million remaining in cash investment accounts for general corporate purposes, Fraker said on the call. In Q3, the REIT acquired Camden Brandon, a 296-unit property in Tampa; Camden LoSo, a 343-unit property in Charlotte, North Carolina; and Camden Gulch, a 300-unit property in Nashville, Tennessee, for a combined $305.2 million, according to the release. Camden acquired a land parcel in Tampa for approximately $18.3 million and sold 2.6 acres of land in Los Angeles for approximately $10.7 million, according to the release. Camden canceled the purchase of two properties and one land parcel in Q3 after interest rates rose , according to Jessett. “We went back looking for price adjustments, and clearly the sellers were not quite willing to capitulate to what we were looking for,” Jessett said. The REIT has also decided not to move forward with Nashville and Denver development projects at this time. Experts Jodie Poirier President, Occupier Services & Agency Leasing Chris Zlocki Global Head of Enterprise Client Strategy & Solutions | Global Occupier Services Bret Swango Senior Vice President, Workforce Analytics & Location Strategy Share Article Location strategy is undergoing a profound transformation. Economic uncertainty, geopolitical disruption, shifting workforce expectations, and rapid technological advancement are forcing organizations to rethink not only where they operate, but how location decisions support broader business priorities. To better understand these shifts, Colliers partnered with CoreNet Global to survey more than 140 corporate real estate professionals from around the world. The findings reveal that location strategy has evolved from a transactional real estate function into a strategic business discipline sitting at the intersection of talent, growth, resilience, and operational performance. The research also uncovered several important trends shaping the future of corporate location strategy. Below are some of the key findings. Talent still leads, but the definition of ‘talent market' is changing Talent remains a primary driver of location decisions. When asked which aspects of location strategy most influence talent outcomes, respondents ranked quality of talent and educational institutions (61%) and commute/accessibility (60%) as the most important considerations. Cost of living, quality of life, and market reputation also ranked highly. According to the report, organizations are increasingly considering employee experience, affordability, and lifestyle factors alongside access to skilled talent. Growth expectations shift toward Asia Pacific Asia Pacific was identified as the region most likely to experience net new portfolio growth over the next three to five years (52%), followed by North America (30%). Additionally, 15% of respondents indicated they do not expect any planned geographic expansion. The report notes that organizations continue to view Asia Pacific as a key destination for expansion, while North America remains an important market for growth, investment, and business activity. Location strategy has evolved as an enterprise decision Respondents identified revenue growth, AI and automation adoption, cost reduction, and talent acquisition and retention among the leading business priorities influencing decision-making over the next 24 months. The survey highlights growing alignment between location strategy and broader enterprise objectives. Reducing operating costs was identified as the top expected contribution of real estate portfolios over the next 24 months, with 64% of respondents selecting it as a priority. Other key priorities include improving employee experience and supporting business growth. Confidence remains high despite rising complexity More than two-thirds of respondents reported being very or somewhat confident in their organization's ability to make long-term location decisions despite ongoing change and uncertainty. Open-ended responses highlighted recurring concerns around cost pressures, market volatility, talent availability, geopolitical risk, and the need for future flexibility. Expert perspective The results of this survey demonstrate that organizations are becoming more sophisticated and strategic in how they evaluate locations. items.title: Lenders turn to cuts, AI as strong jobs point to rate hikes
items.description: Lenders turn to cuts, AI as strong jobs point to rate hikes By Bonnie Sinnock CloseText About Bonnie twitter bcynic mailto bonnie.sinnock@arizent.com linkedin bonnie-sinnock-115a829 Published November 06, 2026, 1:38 p.m. EST | Updated November 06, 2026, 3:35 p.m. EST 3 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Key Insight: Discover why nonbank mortgage payrolls hit a 2026 low despite rising retail productivity gains. Expert Quote: "For housing, stronger hiring cuts both ways." — Sam Williamson, Senior Economist, First American. Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. Nonbank mortgage payroll estimates dropped to a low for 2026 ahead of broader employment gains last month, pointing to a persistent need to manage origination staffing with retail productivity initiatives that have not yet reduced costs but at least contained them. Processing Content Industry-specific data the Bureau of Labor Statistics released with a one-month lag for real-estate credit and loan brokers, when combined, show industry payrolls dropped to 265,100 in August, marking the lowest point since the seasonally-slow first quarter. The statistics, combined with October's strong jobs report signaling a likelihood rates won't immediately fall further , suggest the industry is reducing origination staffing but are able to do so gradually as artificial intelligence has helped boost the number of loans closers handle. "There are a lot of learnings that can happen in this tighter market,'" Walter Mullen, chief strategy officer at Onity , said at IMN's mortgage servicing rights conference this week, noting that origination declines have forced companies to broadly explore operational innovation. Where retail fulfillment productivity stands The number of loans handled by full-time equivalent employees in retail fulfillment have inched up this year primarily due to a surge in closer gains, according to data the Mortgage Bankers Association and Stratmor Group have collected from lenders. The average monthly number of loans per closer jumped from 36.7 to 41.5 between 2025 and 2026 while lenders reported a far more modest gain for processors and a slight decline in productivity in underwriting in line with the more challenging origination environment. Lenders reported a mix of artificial intelligence and leaner staffing drove the productivity gains, which did not reduce costs but have prevented them from rising. Current employment trends: A mixed blessing While the latest industry-specific and total job numbers point to some challenges for mortgage companies, housing economists noted they do point to some offsetting positives for lenders too. "For housing, stronger hiring cuts both ways. More jobs mean more income and more reasons to move, while a stronger economy could prolong the wait for mortgage-rate relief," Sam Williamson, senior economist at First American, wrote in an emailed press statement. October's stronger-than-anticipated gain of 165,000 and a decline in the unemployment rate from 4.2% to 4.1% came with wage gains, according to Williamson. However, MBA noted that there also were indications in the numbers that some workers are underemployed. "While the headline unemployment rate decreased, some of this was due to individuals taking part-time work when they would have preferred a full-time position," MBA Chief Economist Mike Fratantoni wrote in his emailed statement. Despite some signs of weakness like this, Frantantoni said he still anticipates that the overall impact of the numbers will be an increased likelihood that the Federal Open Market Committee will raise short-term rates at one of two of its next meetings. "A resilient job market, combined with inflation that is still too high, is likely to lead the FOMC to hike rates in December. MBA anticipates another hike as well in the first quarter of 2027," he said. While the short-term rates the Fed controls have some bearing on long-term mortgage rates that currently dominate the housing market, mortgage spreads also drive the cost of funds for homebuyers. items.title: Mortgage Rates Drop From September Highs as Midterms and Jobs Data Loom
items.description: Mortgage Rates Drop From September Highs as Midterms and Jobs Data Loom Published on November 2nd, 2026 by Chen Zhao In A Nutshell: Rates have fallen about 30–40 basis points since the peak at the end of September and there’s little reason to believe the volatility will slow down. Last Week’s Highlights The Fed meeting last Wednesday was the highlight of the week, with the committee voting to hold rates steady as expected. There were two dissents, with one coming from a surprising source, Governor Lisa Cook, who is usually seen as someone who favors lower rates. The statement and press conference reiterated a desire to keep hiking, making a December hike more likely than not if the economic data comes in as expected. The Fed has been highlighting elevated inflation and strong economic growth as its reason for hiking. And Q3 GDP, in fact, came in at a brisk 3.4% annual rate. Real business fixed investment spending grew at a 12.7% annual rate thanks to rapid growth in AI spending. And real consumption grew at a 3.8% annual rate as people spent out of savings and wealth increases rather than income growth. The question now is what happens to growth in Q4. Real-time data is pointing to a potential slowdown as consumers pull back. Upcoming Attractions It’s another big week with both the midterm election tomorrow and employment data arriving throughout the week. Democrats are expected to comfortably gain a majority in the House of Representatives with control of the Senate also favoring Democrats, but less certain. Expectations for government spending, which has been a factor for rates, could certainly change with a more divided government. But the near term economic impact might be felt most acutely as we near government funding and debt limit deadlines. The closest budget deadline is December 11, which might get pushed to Q1. And we’re likely to hit the debt limit again in Q1 at which point the Treasury will take “extraordinary measures” until we truly run out of options sometime before October 2027. Since it’s the first week of the month, we’ll also get the typical employment reports, including job openings and turnover on Tuesday and the official jobs report on Friday. With the Fed squarely focused on inflation, the jobs report mostly serves as a check on whether the Fed needs to turn its attention back to recession risk, which would reduce the need for the rate hikes that markets have priced in. So far this year, the answer has been “no,” with the labor market on solid enough footing and that is not expected to change with this week’s data. Finally, Fed officials are out of their blackout period following last week’s FOMC meeting. With Chairman Warsh typically reluctant to offer much forward guidance, markets have been relying more on surrogates to forecast the outcome of the next meeting. There are numerous speaking engagements on the calendar, including Cleveland Fed President Hammack and Dallas Fed President Logan on Thursday, and New York Fed President Williams on Friday. Forecasters will be looking for clues to support the “hike every other meeting” thesis. items.description: AMH Reports Third Quarter 2026 Financial and Operating Results November 4, 2026 Download (opens in new window) Raises Full Year 2026 Guidance LAS VEGAS , Nov. 4, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- AMH (NYSE: AMH) (the "Company"), a leading large-scale integrated owner, operator and developer of single-family rental homes, today announced its financial and operating results for the quarter ended September 30, 2026. Highlights Rents and other single-family property revenues increased 4.1% year-over-year to $498.1 million for the third quarter of 2026. Net income attributable to common shareholders totaled $82.3 million, or $0.23 per diluted share, for the third quarter of 2026, compared to $99.7 million, or $0.27 per diluted share, for the third quarter of 2025. Core Funds from Operations ("Core FFO") attributable to common share and unit holders increased 7.4% year-over-year to $0.50 per FFO share and unit for the third quarter of 2026 and Adjusted Funds from Operations ("Adjusted FFO") attributable to common share and unit holders increased 7.6% year-over-year to $0.45 per FFO share and unit for the third quarter of 2026. Core Net Operating Income ("Core NOI") from Same-Home properties increased by 2.5% year-over-year for the third quarter of 2026. Achieved Same-Home Average Occupied Days Percentage of 96.0% in the third quarter of 2026, while generating 2.6% blended rate growth driven by lease spreads of 3.3% and 1.0% on renewals and new leases, respectively. October 2026 leasing results remained seasonally strong with Same-Home Average Occupied Days Percentage of 96.0%, rate growth on new leases of 0.1% and rate growth on renewals of 3.3%. Delivered a total of 498 high-quality and energy-efficient newly constructed homes from our AMH Development Program to our wholly-owned portfolio and unconsolidated joint ventures in the third quarter of 2026. Repurchased and retired 2.4 million of our outstanding Class A common shares at a weighted-average price of $31.39 per share and a total price of $75.0 million in the third quarter of 2026. Raised Full Year 2026 Core FFO attributable to common share and unit holders guidance midpoint by $0.02 per share and unit to $1.97, representing anticipated full year growth of 5.3% over prior year. "AMH had another strong quarter with balanced execution across the platform and resilient demand driving an increase to the midpoint of our Core FFO per share guidance by $0.02 to $1.97 – now representing 5.3% year-over-year growth," stated Bryan Smith, AMH's Chief Executive Officer. "Our high-quality homes in great locations, superior resident experience supported by our technology and data platform, and outstanding team continue to differentiate AMH and drive sector-leading growth as we close out 2026 and turn our attention to 2027." Third Quarter 2026 Financial Results Net income attributable to common shareholders totaled $82.3 million, or $0.23 per diluted share, for the third quarter of 2026, compared to $99.7 million, or $0.27 per diluted share, for the third quarter of 2025. The decrease was primarily due to lower net gains on property sales and lower other income and expense, net, partially offset by increases in rents and other single-family property revenues exceeding increases in total expenses. On a per diluted share basis, the decrease was partially offset by lower share counts as a result of our share repurchase activity. Rents and other single-family property revenues increased 4.1% to $498.1 million for the third quarter of 2026, compared to $478.5 million for the third quarter of 2025. Revenue growth was primarily driven by higher rental rates. Core NOI from our total portfolio increased 5.3% to $278.4 million for the third quarter of 2026, compared to $264.3 million for the third quarter of 2025. This growth was driven by a 3.6% increase in core revenues resulting primarily from higher rental rates, partially offset by a 0.3% increase in core property operating expenses. For the Company's Same-Home portfolio, core revenues increased 2.3% to $371.1 million for the third quarter of 2026, compared to $362.8 million for the third quarter of 2025, which was driven by a 2.4% increase in Average Monthly Realized Rent per property, partially offset by a 30 basis point decrease in Average Occupied Days Percentage. Core property operating expenses from Same-Home properties increased 1.8% to $125.2 million for the third quarter of 2026, compared to $122.9 million for the third quarter of 2025, primarily driven by higher repairs and maintenance ("R&M") and turnover costs, net. As a result, Core NOI from Same-Home properties increased 2.5% to $246.0 million for the third quarter of 2026, compared to $239.9 million for the third quarter of 2025. items.title: ULI Emerging Trends Report: DFW Three-Peats as Top Market to Watch in 2027, Houston Holds Serve
items.description: ULI Emerging Trends Report: DFW Three-Peats as Top Market to Watch in 2027, Houston Holds Serve by Taylor Williams November 6, 2026 November 6, 2026 4 LAS VEGAS — For the third consecutive year, Dallas-Fort Worth (DFW) has secured the top spot as the U.S. market with the best overall real estate prospects. That’s according to the Emerging Trends in Real Estate 2027 report, which is jointly produced every year by the Urban Land Institute (ULI) and accounting firm PwC. After finishing third and fifth in the 2025 and 2026 rankings, respectively, Houston has more or less maintained the status quo, claiming the No. 6 ranking in the 2027 report. Austin, meanwhile, continued to slip in the rankings, ostensibly due to the market’s ongoing struggles to catch up to recent building booms in the industrial and multifamily sectors. The state capital’s real estate prospects ranked 21st on this year’s list, marking the third consecutive year in which the market has failed to crack the Top 10. In explaining the top ranking, ULI and PwC immediately pointed to t he Texas Stock Exchange (TXSE) , which launched in downtown Dallas earlier this year and has been credited with fueling the growth of a major new vertical within the local economy: financial services. The report identified two nameless financial institutions — known within the real estate community to be Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley — that are developing new office campuses in Uptown Dallas in conjunction with the debut of TXSE. According to the report, combined, these projects could bring as many as 8,800 new jobs to Dallas over the next decade. items.title: 'Certainty Will Be The Buzzword': Stability, Not Sea Change, For CRE Post-Midterm
items.description: The implications of an overwhelming Democratic midterm victory reverberated through markets in the second half of last week, reflecting skittishness among investors and business leaders over fears about the impact on the largest driver of today's economy: data center growth. Despite these initial shocks, there is a quiet expectation that a Democratic Congress will help bring calm to a period of significant economic volatility stemming in part from the unpredictable policymaking that has emerged during President Donald Trump 's second term. “Maybe ‘uncertainty’ was the buzzword of the last year, and hopefully ‘certainty’ will be the buzzword going forward,” said Jeff DeBoer , CEO of the Washington, D.C.-based trade group The Real Estate Roundtable . “We're much more certain that we're not going to wake up every day and have another wild fluctuation in some sort of policy.” Unsplash/Sebastian Schuster That semblance of certainty won't be a panacea, however. Major relief from the ubiquitous issues for commercial real estate today, including higher costs, low labor availability and expensive debt, is unlikely to come from the new Congress because those issues are closely tied to Trump's executive actions and powers. But housing affordability, the economy more generally and data centers were on the ballot in races around the country, where the results have set the stage for a string of policy debates that will hit landlords and investors. “If you look back in history, there are a number of examples where a great amount of very positive legislation has been done when there's divided government,” DeBoer said. “I'm not one who says, ‘Put your feet up, nothing's going to happen, we're in for gridlock.’ I think there's going to be some significant legislation.” Stock traders initially reacted positively to the midterm results, with all three major indexes climbing, but the mood changed Thursday. A massive sell-off focused on tech stocks but spread marketwide sucked $2.5T in market value out of the Nasdaq and pushed the index into correction territory. By Friday, the dust had settled and markets opened by gaining back some of Thursday’s losses. Investors are trying to reprice their bets on the pace of the artificial intelligence infrastructure build-out as they weigh the prospect of a Congress that is more skeptical of the major tech firms’ plans and a wave of local fervor against data centers that drove voters to the polls. AI and data centers emerged as a key political flashpoint, with more than half of respondents telling an NBC exit poll that it was a crucial or major factor in their decision to vote in the midterms. Across statewide races and referendums, voters roundly supported measures putting limits on data center development in more than 40 local ballot measures . “This election, whether federally or on the local level, was influenced by data centers,” said Commercial Real Estate Development Association CEO Marc Selvitelli. “This was the rare bipartisan issue that was out there right now.” The economy emerged as the top issue for voters headed into the election after the U.S. war with Iran drove up energy costs and added to already elevated inflation. The president’s tariffs are also contributing to the rising costs, but the Democratic sweep in Congress still has limited reach into trade policy that’s coming directly from the White House. "The swing in Congress, the results of the election, are very unlikely to have a significant impact on the president's trade agenda and the tariffs that are in place," Blake Harden, managing director for trade policy at ​ Ernst & Young 's Washington Council office, told Reuters . "This is because there is so much trade authority within the executive branch that's been delegated by Congress." Unsplash/Jesse Paul Democrats have floated the idea of changing the tariff laws the president is relying on to impose his protectionist trade regime, but the party would need to win over some Republicans because it remains short of a veto-proof majority. They’re also working on a plan to roll back Trump’s tariffs directed at Canada, The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday. “The midterm election results are unlikely to materially influence commercial real estate performance,” Cushman & Wakefield analysts wrote in a postelection report . A divided government adds some degree of fiscal policy stability that “should be calming for markets,” although the U.S. war in Iran and the downstream impacts on prices and inflation remain the greatest “swing factor for inflation and rates,” they wrote. The election was at least in part a referendum on the war in Iran, according to Hans Nordby , executive managing director of research and investment analytics at Transwestern . “And it was a ‘no’ vote,” Nordby wrote in an email to Bisnow on Friday. “The new Congress could defund the war or otherwise force a withdrawal. If that were to happen, it would seem likely that oil prices could retreat to prewar levels, which would put downward pressure on inflation.” The war and its economic fallout, particularly on the price of oil, has been a thorn in CRE's side since it broke out in February. The rising cost of oil has contributed to overall inflation remaining elevated, which in turn has kept borrowing rates higher. Yields for 10-year U.S. Treasury bonds , a key benchmark rate for all sorts of debt costs, notched lower following the midterms after climbing above 5% in October before retreating, shedding 6 basis points Wednesday and continuing to trade below 4.9% through Friday. The shift in Congress likely sets the stage for bitter political fights between Trump and Democrats, some of whom have pledged to launch investigations into the White House. items.title: What Each Party Promises on Housing Affordability as Congress Hangs in the Balance – Realtor.com
items.description: As they jockey for control of Congress in a tight midterm race, Democrats and Republicans have each made promises that their party will focus on housing affordability. Both parties have spent the year pushing messages about affordability, especially in housing. Homeowners are being hammered with higher insurance and property tax rates . Higher interest rates have frozen the housing market . And young people are overwhelmingly concerned about whether they'll ever own a home at all. With many close races, control of Congress could hinge on these concerns. Then there's the issue of how to implement laws Congress has already passed. The bipartisan 21st Century Road to Housing Act promises reforms in dozens of provisions aimed at cutting red tape and encouraging the construction of more homes. Congress will oversee the rollout of those new programs while also working with the final two years of the Trump administration—and the market will be looking to Washington for clarity. Jeff Holzmann , COO of Dallas-based real estate firm RREAF, tells Realtor.com® the industry needs clear rules to make long-term investment decisions. Broad rules such as the new ban on institutional investors in the housing market require clarity or else they might not achieve the affordability Congress intended with the bill. "From my operator's perspective, the bigger question is whether these regulations will continue to encourage private capital to invest in building new homes and improving existing ones, as that's what drives our business," Holzmann says. "If that pans out, I believe it can make a real difference in affordability over time." What Republicans Want Over the course of the year, many Republicans have said they want to see reforms to the housing finance system. These rules, they've said, have discouraged banks and financial institutions from infusing money into the housing market. House Financial Services Committee Chair Rep. French Hill (R- AR ) told the U.S. Chamber of Commerce in September that he wanted to see reforms to the BASEL III framework , aimed to encourage more banks to finance mortgages and construction loans. "That should take steps to encourage the large banks to participate in the secondary market for housing," Hill said. "I think Dodd-Frank went too far on this point. Essentially, by the capital standards for a construction loan, pushed a lot of the biggest banks out of that business. It also limited mortgage servicing rights by the large financial institutions. Both of those things, at the margin, raise the cost of liquidity for housing." Rep. Mike Flood (R- NE ), who chairs the Housing and Insurance Subcommittee, said in July he wants to see single-family homebuilding exempted from the prevailing wage requirements in the Davis-Bacon and Related Acts . Mike Flood of Nebraska, who chairs the Housing and Insurance Subcommittee, at Punchbowl News Summit Panel Discussion on Housing Tristan Navera for Realtor.com Flood and Hill have both said they want to exempt homebuilding materials from the Build America Buy America Act . That adds sourcing requirements to many building materials that drive up their costs. At the same time, Republicans have also backed the Trump administration's shift of the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development away from "housing first" homelessness programs . HUD has repeatedly criticized what Secretary Scott Turner calls a "homeless industrial complex." In alternate, HUD has pursued programs that emphasize treatment and recovery. But it's clashed with states and service providers and pursued "diversity equity and inclusion" programs as well. What Democrats Want Democrats have called for additional spending to help bolster a variety of housing programs, especially those regarding tenant and homeowner protections. Earlier this year, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) said Democrats would pursue laws cracking down on junk fees and on predatory companies abusing tenants and using price-fixing algorithms. A number of Democrat-led bills this year have also proposed expanding funding for Section 8 vouchers, rent relief, programs to help curtail evictions, and expansion of the Low-Income Tax Credit, which produces about 40,000 to 50,000 units a year of affordable housing. Rep. Emanuel Cleaver (D-MO), ranking member of the Banking subcommittee, told the Chamber of Commerce in September that both parties must be focused on effective compromise. "We're woefully lacking in legislation that can move through both the House and the Senate and get to the president's desk," he said. Democrats are also likely to resume efforts for stricter data center regulation . They sank a Republican-led bill that encouraged utilities to shield ratepayers from data center costs in favor of a proposal with more stringent enforcement powers for the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission. The party will also have to contend with a wave of Democratic Socialist candidates elected at the local and state level. Those candidates have shown different levels of support for policies like rent control and " housing for all ." What's bipartisan? The 43-member bipartisan Build America Caucus put out a 95-page primer for issues it would pursue regardless of who is in control of either chamber next year. Its housing agenda includes fast-tracking residential construction in areas where cities have "outdated" zoning constraints in place. It also wants to see programs that encourage housing near transit and under-used federal land, as well as modernization of building code standards. “The problem isn't a lack of good ideas; it's the bureaucratic red tape slowing projects down for years," Rep.
