items.title: Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac rally as Ackman presses for conservatorship exit
items.description: Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points The midterm elections could be a turning point for the release of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac from government control, according to Bill Ackman. Both stocks have moved more than 60% higher since Oct. 14. Ackman believes both names can see a "10-fold" increase from current share prices. Bill Ackman, chief executive officer of Pershing Square Capital Management LP, center, during the company's initial public offering (IPO) on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York, US, on Wednesday, April 29, 2026. Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty Images The midterm elections could be a turning point for the release of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac from government control, according to billionaire investor Bill Ackman. Investors may agree with him, if the rally in both stocks is any sign. The Federal National Mortgage Association, known as Fannie Mae, and Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corporation, or Freddie Mac, have each jumped more than 60% from Oct. 14 to Monday's close. The stocks were both up roughly 3% on Tuesday. Ackman, the founder of Pershing Square Capital Management, has long pushed for the two entities to be released from federal conservatorship. "The reason why it's not being touched right now is, you know, midterms," he said in an interview with CNBC's " Squawk Box ." Federal National Mortgage Association (Fannie Mae) and Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corporation (Freddie Mac) over the last month. Ackman, who owns both names through Pershing Square, believes Freddie and Fannie have the potential to increase "10-fold from current share prices," he said in his quarterly letter to shareholders, issued on Monday. Fannie and Freddie buy mortgages from banks and other lenders, and then package them into mortgage-backed securities, known as MBS. Their operations are critical to the housing market, providing liquidity to banks and creating a secondary market for MBS. The entities were placed into conservatorship in September 2008, during the financial crisis. The stocks were delisted from the New York Stock Exchange in 2010 and have traded over the counter since then. Ackman wants the conservatorship to end, arguing the entities would be worth multiples of their current valuation if they were freed from government control. VIDEO 22:14 22:14 Watch CNBC's full interview with Bill Ackman, Pershing Square CEO President Donald Trump has supported ending the conservatorship of Fannie and Freddie. But it remains politically and economically contentious. The entities operate under strict capital threshold requirements and would need to be recapitalized, which could happen through issuing common equity. However, the Treasury Department would need to figure out an exit plan for its roughly $388 billion ownership stake in the entities through preferred securities and warrants. Congress may also need to play a role, passing legislation to restructure the government's role in mortgage financing and home-loan guarantees. Nonetheless, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent recently said it could happen before Trump's term ends, telling 2Way's " The Morning Meeting " podcast that the administration will tackle the ownership structure "next year, the year after." He said affordability will be guiding the decision. One point of controversy is whether ending the conservatorship of Fannie and Freddie would increase the spreads on MBS over Treasuries, effectively making mortgages costlier. Bessent has sought to reassure the market that wouldn't happen. "Whatever we do is going to be guided by making sure that the spread on [agency] mortgages … over the Treasury does not increase," Bessent said. Ackman argues that privatizing the GSEs would help insulate them from political meddling. "Fannie and Freddie are these massive, enormously profitable institutions where whichever political party controls them…if they're still in conservatorship, can influence the outcome of elections," he told CNBC. In one scenario, he explained, Democrats win the White House, conservatorship is still in place, and Democrats push Fannie and Freddie to lower credit standards in order to expand home ownership and affordability. "If they're going to move more aggressively into borrowers with lower credit quality, for example, to achieve a political objective, that's going to have an impact on trillions of dollars outstanding mortgage securities," Ackman said. "It's going to have an impact on overall credit spreads." MBS investors want certainty about how the entities will be run, he noted. "That only gets resolved in a world in which they exit conservatorship, they become publicly traded companies that are owned by institutional and retail investors," Ackman said. "We set the rules. items.title: Why didn’t the strong jobs report send mortgage rates skyrocketing?
items.description: With all the crazy things happening this week, the blowout jobs report on Friday didn’t send mortgage rates up at all. But one thing is for sure: the labor market has been better in 2026 than it was in 2025. I once labelled the labor market the honey badger labor market and no matter what has been thrown at the U.S. economy after 2011 — outside the brief recession created by COVID-19 — the labor data has held up well. Let’s dig into why very strong jobs report didn’t push yields or mortgage rates higher, as we would normally expect with the Fed being so hawkish in their statement. From BLS : Total nonfarm payroll employment rose by 165,000 in October, and the unemployment rate changed little at 4.1 percent, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today. Employment increased in professional and business services, in health care, and in transportation and warehousing. The labor data has improved enough that we have gone from a 4.5% unemployment rate last year to 4.1% today. Part of this is that labor-force growth has slowed and the break-even number has decreased, meaning fewer jobs are needed to keep the unemployment rate low. I have my break-even at 78,000 jobs created per month; I believe the Fed's is 33,000. Some economists have it at zero, which I think is silly. In any case, the unemployment rate is lower this year versus last year. Now, the low point in the COVID-19 recovery was about 3.4% unemployment back in 2023, so the unemployment rate has increased from that low, but it's still good enough to keep the Fed’s focus on inflation instead of labor. Jobs breakdown This month's report had growth in a few sectors, especially the business services sector jobs with one of the biggest monthly prints in years. There was also growth in manufacturing, and transportation & warehouse, while construction jobs faded a tad. Construction labor will be interesting in the future if mortgage rates stay elevated and short-term rates go up. If there is an AI slowdown and fewer AI data centers are being built, will this sector start to decline? One of my most critical recession indicators, residential construction employment, doesn’t look great lately, but it isn’t looking terrible either. In previous cycles, you can see a clear downtrend in this labor pool, which hasn’t happened in this cycle. With builders doing more rate buydowns — which have kept new home sales at 2019 levels over the past few years — and remodeling work holding up, this clear recession indicator hasn’t broken yet. 10-year yield and mortgage rates As crazy as this week has been, the jobs data wasn’t the big driver of mortgage rates as much as AI stock prices. CoreWeave's stock price was up 10% pre-market today, and bond yields ticked up with that. The jobs report didn’t do much to yields, we just saw a mild increase and then they fell back in line with the trend. Then CoreWeave stock price went almost negative, bond yields fell to the lows of the day, and now both have picked up from the lows! The market needs a weekend break. Mortgage rates ended the day flat at 7.17%, so as crazy as this sounds, the blowout jobs data didn’t send mortgage rates or bond yields much higher. That's good news for rates, and there are some levers the new Congress can pull to potentially get rates even lower, which I discussed on today's episode of the HousingWire Daily podcast with Editor in Chief Sarah Wheeler. Conclusion A lot has changed this week for the economy regarding the bond market and where mortgage rates can go. The blue wave has raised hopes that the trade war and the conflict with Iran can end soon, AI companies have shown they can bleed, and Congress will try to slow the AI boom as much as it can without crashing it. All these things happened this week, so that even with four solid jobs reports during jobs week, the 10-year yield closed at 4.86% and mortgage rates closed at weekly lows. Related More: Jobs Report

items.description: Opportunity Zone Home Price Growth Largely Tracks Other Areas by ATTOM Team | Nov 5, 2026 | Home Sales & Prices , Real Estate News - Recent Articles Median home prices grew year-over-year in 48.9 percent of Opportunity Zone census tracts, compared to 51.6 percent of tracts outside the zones. IRVINE, Cal. — Nov. 5, 2026 — ATTOM , the leading provider of property data , AI-powered intelligence , and real estate analytics solutions, today released its third-quarter 2026 report analyzing qualified low-income Opportunity Zones targeted by Congress for economic redevelopment in the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 (see full methodology below). In this report, ATTOM looked at 3,805 census tracts in Opportunity Zones around the United States with sufficient data to analyze, meaning they had at least five home sales in the third quarter of the year. Median single-family home and condo prices rose quarter-over-quarter in 48.1 percent (1,651) of the 3,431 Opportunity Zone tracts with sufficient data in both the second and third quarter. Year-over-year, home prices rose in 48.9 percent (1,598) of the 3,265 tracts with sufficient data in the third quarters of 2025 and 2026. Typical home prices rose year-over-year in 51.6 percent (28,212) of the 54,704 census tracts outside of Opportunity Zones with sufficient data in both quarters to be included in the analysis, meaning that price growth was more common outside the targeted economic development zones than inside them. In 9.4 percent (357) of Opportunity Zone census tracts, the third quarter of 2026 marked the highest median home value since the beginning of the Great Recession in 2008 and 27.1 percent of the Opportunity Zone census tracts experienced double-digit growth in home values year-over-year. “Opportunity Zones remain a notably lower-cost segment of the housing market, with nearly 80 percent of these areas posting median home prices below the national median,” said Rob Barber, CEO of ATTOM. “Even so , home values were only slightly less likely to rise in these areas in the third quarter, suggesting that many of these communities are still moving broadly with the market.” The national median home sales price in the third quarter was $368,000. Inside Opportunity Zones, 79.5 percent of census tracts in ATTOM’s analysis had typical home prices below the national median. Outside the zones, only 50.4 percent of census tracts in the analysis had typical prices below the national median. Due to the small number of sales in many Opportunity Zone census tracts, median price measurements can be volatile. The typical median sales price rose or fell by more than 5 percent quarter-over-quarter in 79.1 percent of the 3,431 tracts with sufficient data in the second and third quarters. items.title: Gateway Markets Regain Development Momentum
items.description: Gateway Markets Regain Development Momentum by Chuck Ehmann Posted October 29, 2026 in Multifamily Construction Permits Whether you call them “gateway” markets or the “sexy six,” the primary coastal hubs that traditionally attract the majority of domestic and international capital are well represented among the top markets for annual multifamily permitting in September’s data release from the U.S. Census Bureau, and in most cases are dramatically increasing their permitting activity. New York continues to lead the nation for multifamily permitting with 37,691 units permitted in the year-ending September, an increase of more than 13,000 units from last year or a jump of 52.7%. Los Angeles again ranked #2 with about 18,000 units permitted, almost doubling their annual total from one year ago. Washington, DC remained among the top permitting markets at #5 in September, increasing their annual permitting by 47.4% or about 3,900 units, while Seattle slipped to #11 this month but still increased their multifamily permitting total by 36.7% or roughly 2,400 units. Rounding out the “sexy six,” Boston ranked #16 among Realpage’s top 150 markets with a 44.7% annual increase (+2,303 units) to 7,460 units, while the Bay Area markets of San Jose, Oakland and San Francisco ranked well down the list individually but would have ranked #7 with a combined total of 11,543 units permitted, up 46.8% from last year (+5,407 units). Conversely, among the secondary high-growth markets, development activity has stalled or fallen back as top 10 markets Phoenix and Atlanta permitted close to the same amount as last year, while Dallas, Houston, Austin and Miami decreased their permitted unit counts by a combined 11,004 units. Only Raleigh/Durham saw a significant increase in multifamily permitting (+3,153 units) among the non-gateway top 10 markets. Despite declining permitting in four of September’s top 10 markets, their combined total of 148,456 units was up 14.5% from last September for an increase of 18,765 units. Compared to August, the top 10 markets’ annual permitting total was little changed (-0.7%). In addition to the expanding top 10 and the gateway markets mentioned, other markets with significant increases in annual units permitted in September were Kansas City (+2,187 units), West Palm Beach (+1,932 units), College Station-Bryan, TX (+1,762 units), Tacoma (+1,712 units) and Fort Worth (+1,672 units). Orlando (-4,572 units) led for annual permitting decreases, followed by Dallas and Houston. Significant decreases occurred in Columbus, OH (-2,911 units), Riverside-San Bernardino (-2,162 units), San Diego (-2,100 units) and Lakeland-Winter Haven, FL (-1,995 units). Permitting by Place Below the metro level, eight of August’s top 10 permit-issuing places returned to this month’s list with the first five remaining in order. The list of top individual permitting places (cities, towns, boroughs, and unincorporated counties) generally includes the principal city of some of the most active metro areas. The city of Los Angeles again led the nation for multifamily permitting at the local level with New York’s three most active boroughs returning among the top five. The city of Phoenix also placed in the top five while the city of Fort Worth jumped to #6 in September from #10 last month. The cities of Austin and Atlanta each slipped one spot as the cities of Columbus and Houston fell out of the top 10 entirely. The cities of Miami and Denver joined the top 10 list this month, permitting about 5,500 units apiece. Among the top 10 metros for multifamily permitting, Dallas, Houston, Washington, DC and Raleigh/Durham were not represented on the top 10 list of permitting places, although the core cities of Dallas, Houston, Raleigh and Durham were among the top 20 places. Washington, DC’s multifamily permitting was spread diversely around that metro’s area. items.title: Can the new Congress help lower mortgage rates?
items.description: After the Democrats' historic midterm win , the question now is: can the new Congress help get mortgage rates lower? Obviously, the Iran conflict and trade war have taken their toll on President Trump's approval ratings, but can Congress — both Democrats and Republicans — now work together on getting something done that the President will not veto? Let's look at the economic factors influencing rates in this environment, what Congress can do about each, and how the Fed might consider these as they set monetary policy. 1. Oil and diesel prices When WTI oil was at $112 on April 7 this year, the 10-year yield was at 4.31% — but back then the Fed was still talking about cutting rates two to three times. A lot has changed since then. The Federal Reserve has made the Iran conflict a big talking point, so some type of resolution to this conflict could impact rates. Obviously, the conflict has hurt President Trump and the Republicans; it’s very unpopular, especially with farmers and truckers who have to deal with high diesel prices. Trump himself acknowledged the war played a major part in the midterm results. Congress made some attempts to try to end this conflict in the past, but may have renewed incentives now to find a solution. We shall see what comes next, as President Trump has said he could make a deal after the midterms. 2. The AI boom Now, the AI boom is a little bit more complicated because there are a lot of projects still in the pipeline that can’t be shut down by the Democrats right now, but future projects could definitely be affected. And with some type of regulation and moratorium, some of the growth prospects might be slowed down. This is a critical factor because the Federal Reserve has really made the AI boom and inflation a hot topic. It’s part of the reason why, when you see AI softness — whether it’s the credit markets or their stock prices getting hit — bond traders tend to want to buy bonds, not sell them, in that environment. For now, the Fed needs to see a material slowdown to lose its hawkish stance on AI, but it would be another positive for rates. On another note, the labor productivity data was awesome today. This data really affects how the Fed sees AI and will be the best news for mortgage rates if this trend continues. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh himself has made a dovish case around AI as long as it creates more productivity and lowers labor unit costs. Here is the chart of the 10-year yield for the last six months as of this second, the 10-year yield is down once again to 4.83% as AI stocks are selling off. 3. Trade war 2.0 This will be very interesting because I am sure President Trump will try every legal angle to continue his tariff policy — he still wants to have tariffs because it’s his favorite tool to cut deals. However, what the midterms have done is limit the power he can have to escalate the trade war into something worse. That can be a very big positive: we might have seen the high of the 10-year yield at 5.35% if the trade war doesn’t get worse amid the conflict with Iran. For now, we need to wait and see how much farther the President wants to push the trade war. He might just cut a deal with Canada, leave other countries alone and just focus on China — which would be a positive for rates. 4. Jobs Usually, in an economic cycle, when manufacturing jobs and construction jobs are being lost, it’s not a good sign for the labor market: we saw that in 2025. But the labor market has improved this year and that has kept the Fed's focus fully on inflation. One thing to think about going forward is that, if we do have some data center moratoriums and rates stay elevated, construction labor might get hit a little bit harder than before the midterms. If the unemployment rate rises as growth slows down, that will be a positive for mortgage rates. Conclusion For rates to really make a meaningful move lower and stick, three of the four things above need to get better. You need to get oil prices trading between $67 and $82. You need to get diesel prices down so the Fed won’t talk about energy prices being passed onto the consumer. You've got to de-escalate the trade war 2.0 and get some deals in and not make it inflationary. The AI moratorium and regulations will be a welcome signal to the Federal Reserve; whether that impacts the construction data enough to matter to them is still an open question, but the three things above need to occur to have rates go under 7% and stay there. items.title: Realpage Economy Express Episode 74
items.description: Realpage Economy Express Episode 74 by Arben Skivjani Posted October 30, 2026 in Insights The Fed held rates steady, but two dissenters wanted a hike now, and strong growth and rising inflation are keeping a December increase firmly on the table. The Federal Reserve held rates steady in a 10-to-2 vote, with both dissenters wanting an immediate quarter-point hike. Its statement also upgraded growth to strong and called inflation still elevated, while Warsh declined to commit on December until he sees more data. Fed funds futures now put the odds of a December hike at about 82%, down slightly after Thursday's data but higher than a week ago. Thursday's GDP report showed the economy grew 3.4% last quarter, faster than expected, with investment doing more of the lifting than consumers. The Fed's preferred inflation gauge rose 3.6% from a year ago in September, with core climbing to 3.1% and prices jumping 0.5% in a single month. Income and spending figures for September show take-home pay fell after inflation and spending went nowhere, with gasoline taking the biggest bite. Consumer surveys diverged, as Conference Board confidence jumped while University of Michigan sentiment barely moved and respondents there expect inflation near 5% over the next year. The National Association of Realtors reported pending home sales at the lowest level on record, as mortgage rates remain above 7% and buyers stay on the sidelines. Housing starts data show apartment starts down about 26% from a year ago, though permits picked up in September, suggesting some builders are lining up projects for later. items.title: San Diego apartment supply is about to peak
items.description: San Diego apartment supply is about to peak by Kim O'Brien Posted November 5, 2026 in Insights San Diego apartment supply hit a record high in the past year and is set to peak in 1st quarter 2027. In the year-ending 3rd quarter 2026, roughly 6,600 units completed across San Diego, marking the highest annual total since Realpage Market Analytics began tracking the market in 2000. Supply in the past year also surpassed the market’s decade average around the 4,000-unit mark. Annual supply in San Diego is expected to remain elevated, peaking in the year-ending 1st quarter 2027, when roughly 6,880 units are scheduled for completion. After that, supply is slated to come down, aligning closer to the market’s decade average by the end of 2027. Demand is keeping pace with record apartment supply in San Diego, as evidenced by occupancy at 95.7% in October and rents up 1.5% year-over-year. After supply hits its peak and starts to come down, this market is projected to see improvement in both of those metrics. items.title: What housing market headlines can't tell your clients
items.description: Mortgage rates are moving closer to 7%, and housing demand is showing signs of stabilizing. But what does that mean for a homeowner preparing to list, a buyer wondering whether to wait or an agent trying to set realistic expectations? In his latest Housing Market Tracker , HousingWire Lead Analyst Logan Mohtashami explains why a path to sub-7% mortgage rates is back on the table. While weekly pending home sales have recently stabilized, that doesn't yet signal a sustained recovery. For housing professionals, the opportunity is to translate those national trends into what clients are experiencing in their own markets. HousingWire Data from Houston, Phoenix and Tampa reveals three things worth watching: Look beyond the headline. A national or regional trend may not reflect the competition your client faces. Watch how the signals move together. Changes in pending sales, inventory and price reductions can reveal where competition may be heading. Recognize when conditions are shifting. Recent market activity can change before the longer-term numbers tell the same story. Look beyond the headline A client sees that housing demand is stabilizing and asks whether it's finally a good time to sell. Houston demonstrates why the answer requires more local context. Across the Houston metro, the ratio of new pending sales to new listings improved during October, but not because buyer activity increased. New listings declined faster than pending sales, making the ratio look stronger even as fewer homes went under contract. Within Houston city limits, the opposite happened. Pending sales declined faster than new listings, pushing the ratio lower. Even inventory told a different story. Active inventory was higher than a year ago across the metro but lower within the city. Neither market showed growing pending activity, yet the conditions affecting buyers and sellers were different. For a homeowner, that distinction matters more than whether a regional headline describes the market as improving. The takeaway: Use broader housing trends to start the conversation, then show clients what's happening among the homes they're actually competing with. A seller needs to understand current competition and buyer activity, not simply whether the overall market appears stronger. Watch how the signals move together A homeowner considering whether to wait for lower mortgage rates might assume that more affordable financing will bring more buyers. But lower rates could also encourage more sellers to list, making the relationship between supply and demand especially important. Phoenix illustrates what happens when several indicators point in the same direction. Over the latest four-week period, new pending sales declined faster than new listings. Compared with a year ago, pending activity was down nearly 17%, while new listings were slightly higher. Meanwhile, active inventory continued to grow, and more than half of active listings had experienced a price reduction. Together, those indicators suggest increasing competition among sellers. Fewer homes are moving into pending status, more inventory is available and price reductions are becoming more prevalent. That doesn't guarantee prices will fall, but it identifies conditions that could create additional pricing pressure if the trend continues. The takeaway: Don't evaluate pending sales, inventory or price reductions in isolation. When several indicators reinforce one another, they provide stronger evidence of where conditions may be headed. That can help sellers evaluate pricing and timing, while giving buyers a clearer picture of their negotiating position. Recognize when conditions are shifting A seller points out that inventory is still lower than last year. Does that mean competition remains limited? Tampa shows why the direction of recent activity matters just as much as the year-over-year comparison. Within Tampa city limits, new listings and pending sales were essentially unchanged over the latest four weeks. Active inventory remained below last year's level, and the share of listings with price reductions had declined. But inventory was also beginning to increase compared with the preceding four weeks. That doesn't establish a market shift. Recent pending activity has been relatively steady, and price-cut share continues to ease. Still, the inventory increase is worth monitoring. If inventory continues building while pending activity remains weak, sellers could face greater competition even before the year-over-year inventory comparison turns positive. Try it yourself: Switch the chart above between 6M and YoY. The six-month view shows how inventory has been building recently, while the year-over-year comparison reveals that inventory remains below last year's levels. Both are true, but each tells you something different about the market. The takeaway: A favorable market statistic doesn't mean conditions are standing still. Track recent changes alongside year-over-year trends, and revisit pricing or buying strategies when the evidence begins to shift. What they need from you is the expertise to explain what those trends mean for their home, their competition and their next decision. items.description: October 2026 Monthly Housing Trends: Buyers and Sellers Hit Pause as Rates Surge By Jake Krimmel Nov 04, 2026 Market outlook If September’s slowdown hinted at a fall stall for the housing market, October confirmed it. Mortgage rates peaked at 7.40% in mid-October, capping a six-week 74 basis point surge. And although rates have since eased to 7.24%, the damage to purchasing power has been done. The same monthly principal and interest payment now supports a loan nearly 6% smaller than it did in late August. The October Realtor.com® data show a market where almost everyone has pressed pause for now. Buyers on the sidelines are staying there, and sellers – whether they’re on or off market – are disengaging as well. New listings fell at their fastest rate in three years, while current sellers are not slashing prices or pulling listings at meaningfully higher rates than last year, when falling mortgage rates kept the market unseasonably warm. What happens next depends on the broader economy. A dip in the 10-year Treasury yield could restore some purchasing power, but it could also tempt buyers to wait for further progress. Our base case is that mortgage rates remain above 7% in the near term, with the market facing an early chill as winter approaches. In This Report Top storylines and key questions Core metrics: October 2026 Summary tables Data appendix October’s top storylines, according to the data Buyers pull back, as they battle mortgage rates and loss of purchasing power Pending sales are down 10.5% year over year, the steepest annual decline since October 2023, and contract signings are also down 17%. With 30-year rates averaging 7.33% in October, 107 basis points above a year ago, buyers have lost real purchasing power. Sellers freeze rather than panic New listings fell 7.5% year over year, the steepest drop since September 2023, but delistings and price cuts are moving sideways. About 4.4% of active listings were delisted, versus 4.6% a year ago, and the share with a price cut (20.5%) is just 0.2 points above last year and down from September. Sellers are disengaging rather than showing signs of real distress. About 43% of current active listings have ever had their price reduced, down from nearly 55% a year ago. Inventory growth accelerates for fourth straight month, closest to pre-pandemic norm yet Active listings grew 7.4% year over year, topping 1.18 million homes for sale, the fourth straight month of faster growth. National inventory sits 6.7% below pre-pandemic norms, the narrowest gap we have seen yet. Key questions Q: Mortgage rates averaged 7.33% in October, the highest since 2023. Where is that showing up in the market, and is the impact the same everywhere? A: Even with rates dipping slightly in the latest reading (7.24% on Oct 29, down from 7.40% in mid-October), 30-year rates are still 107 basis points above this time last year and 53 above the start of September. That loss of purchasing power (a 10.4% loss compared to a year ago and a 5.2% loss since the start of September) is showing up first in the demand indicators. The stock of homes under contract is down about 10.5% year over year, contract signings are down by 17%, and mortgage applications for purchase are down more than 18% from a year ago over the past two weeks. Q: Last month, we said sellers were the thing to watch. Are they responding to weaker demand by cutting prices, pulling listings, or sitting out altogether? A: Right now it looks more like a seller pause than an exodus. For the fourth consecutive month, more than 1 in 5 listings saw a price cut, but the share is only 0.2 points above last year and slipped from September. New listings are down year over year at a time of year when they are already seasonally low. Sellers know this is a poor time to list, and you do not list into weak demand unless you need to. What we have not seen is a meaningful increase in delistings. That matters for two reasons. First, sellers are not giving up yet. And second, we also need to reframe the delisting conversation this time of year, because a higher count, even if it were happening, would not signal seller stress as we approach the holidays. A seller throwing in the towel in July is different from one calling it quits around Halloween or nearing Thanksgiving. Q: What should we be monitoring heading into the holiday months as 2026 comes to a close? A: Prices vs. inventory. More inventory and slower sales mean rising months of supply, but if sellers are not cutting prices more deeply, the market may not be getting as buyer-friendly as the inventory numbers imply. List prices are down 2.2%, the 12th straight year-over-year decline, but with mortgage rates still significantly higher than this time last year, potential buyers are still operating at a loss when it comes to purchasing power. The Realtor.com ® 2026Q3 Market Clock® Report found the US housing market is on the cusp of buyer’s market territory, and about two-thirds of the 100 largest metros were either outright buyer’s markets or trending in that direction. Still, buyers gaining ground at the negotiating table is different from gaining enough purchasing power to pull would-be buyers off the sidelines. Until the affordability math shifts notably, do not expect swings in housing demand. items.title: Single-Family Development Remains Constrained
items.description: Single-Family Development Remains Constrained by Chuck Ehmann Posted October 21, 2026 in Multifamily Construction Permits Don't expect single-family construction to accelerate anytime soon. Consumer and builder confidence has weakened, while mortgage rates, financing costs, construction expenses, labor costs and regulatory hurdles continue to weigh on development activity. At the same time, ongoing affordability concerns and elevated home prices are limiting housing demand. Single-family housing starts surged above 1.3 million units on a seasonally adjusted basis during the post-pandemic period of exceptionally low mortgage rates. As borrowing costs climbed and mortgage rates moved above 7%, housing starts fell to roughly 800,000 units by late 2022. Annualized starts activity later recovered to more than one million units before gradually easing back toward 900,000 units in 2026. With mortgage rates averaging roughly 7.4% in October, pressure on the single-family sector is likely to persist. September’s seasonally adjusted rate for single-family starts was 859,000 units, down 4.6% from August’s revised rate but up 2.6% from one year ago. Annualized single-family permits fell 4% from August and 4.8% from last September to a 3.5-year low of 845,000 units. The number of single-family homes currently under construction was unchanged month-to-month at 587,000 units, but that annualized rate was down 2.8% from last September. Single-family completions dipped 2.4% for the month but fell 11% from one year ago to 840,000 units, while units authorized, but not started jumped 6.3% from last year to 151,000 units, the same rate as last month. Meanwhile, multifamily development faces similar headwinds with the seasonally adjusted starts rate at 349,000 units, down 7.2% from August and 25.9% from last year. Annualized multifamily permitting increased 5.9% for the month and 1% for the year to 503,000 units. Reflecting the volatility of the seasonally adjusted data series, the unadjusted annual starts and permits totals for multifamily were both up close to 7% from last September. Like the single-family series, the annualized rate of multifamily units under construction was unchanged for the month at 677,000 units, however, that was down 3.1% for the year. Authorized multifamily units that were not started were also unchanged for the month at 123,000 units but were up 13.9% for the year. Multifamily completions rose 14.9% from August to 339,000 units but were down 20.4% for the year. Compared to one year ago, the annual rate for multifamily permitting increased in two of the four regions, with moderate improvement in the Northeast (up 8.5% to 83,000 units) and solid growth in the Midwest (up 32.8% to 79,000 units). The West region saw the deepest decrease of 17% in annual multifamily permitting to 100,000 units in September, followed by a very modest 0.2% decrease in the South to 241,000 units. Compared to the previous month, permitting was down in the West and up in the remaining regions. Annualized multifamily starts decreased sharply in three regions: the West (down 56.7% to 48,000 units), the Midwest (down 54.4% to 35,000 units) and the Northeast (down 43.5% to 62,000 units). The South region’s multifamily starts increased 16.8% to 205,000 units. Compared to August’s seasonally adjusted annual rate, starts were up strongly in the South and down in the remaining regions. items.title: Multifamily Developer Confidence Weakens in Third Quarter
items.description: Multifamily Developer Confidence Weakens in Third Quarter November 5, 2026 Eric Lynch No Comments New multifamily housing confidence weakened year-over-year in the third quarter, according to the Multifamily Market Survey (MMS) by the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB). The MMS produces two separate indices. The Multifamily Production Index (MPI) had a reading of 41, down five points year-over-year, while the Multifamily Occupancy Index (MOI) had a reading of 69, also down five points year-over-year. Developer sentiment for new multifamily production has softened, due to challenges such as high interest rates , construction costs that are high relative to rents, and problems getting projects approved and connected to roads and utilities, resulting in many projects taking longer to complete. Due to the headwinds facing the industry, NAHB’s 2027 forecast shows a decline for multifamily starts. Although the administration’s regulatory reform efforts are helping to ease some cost pressures, the multifamily sector would still benefit from an expedited permit process and lower rates on development and construction loans . Multifamily Production Index (MPI) The MMS asks multifamily developers to rate the current conditions as “good ”, “fair”, or “poor” for multifamily starts in markets where they are active. The index and all its components are scaled so that a number above 50 indicates that more respondents report conditions as good rather than poor. The MPI is a weighted average of four key market segments: three in the built-for-rent market (garden/low-rise, mid/high-rise, and subsidized) and the built-for-sale (or condominium) market. All four components experienced decreases year-over-year and are in negative territory (i.e., below 50) during the third quarter. The component measuring subsidized units fell six points to 49, the component measuring garden/low-rise dropped five points to 48, and both the component measuring mid/high-rise units and the component measuring built-for-sale units decreased four points to 33 and 31, respectively. Multifamily Occupancy Index (MOI) The survey also asks multifamily property owners to rate the current conditions for occupancy of existing rental apartments in markets where they are active as “good”, “fair”, or “poor”. Like the MPI, the MOI and all its components are scaled so that a number above 50 indicates more respondents report that occupancy is good than poor. The MOI is a weighted average of three built-for-rent market segments (garden/low-rise, mid/high-rise, and subsidized). Two of the three components experienced declines year-over-year for the third quarter of 2026. The mid/high-rise component declined seven points to 59 and the garden/low-rise component fell six points to 70. The component measuring subsidized units saw an increase of two points to 83. Nevertheless, all three components remained above the break-even point of 50. Changes in Overall Market Conditions The MMS was re-designed in 2023 to produce results that are easier to interpret and consistent with the proven format of other NAHB industry sentiment surveys. Until there is enough data to seasonally adjust the series, changes in the MMS indices should only be evaluated on a year-over-year basis. For more recent information about the market, the survey contains a separate question asking multifamily developers to compare current market conditions to conditions three months earlier. In the third quarter of 2026, 6% of respondents said the current market is better, and 28% said it is worse. However, the majority of developers—66%—said that the market is currently about the same as it was three months ago. Please visit NAHB’s MMS web page for the full report. items.title: Private Residential Construction Slips as Remodeling Weakens
items.description: Private Residential Construction Slips as Remodeling Weakens November 2, 2026 Catherine Koh No Comments Private residential construction spending decreased in September 2026 driven by a steep decline in improvement (remodeling) spending. According to the latest construction spending data from the U.S. Census Bureau, private residential construction spending came in at a seasonally adjusted annual rate (SAAR) of $848.8 billion in September, down 5.5% from the revised August estimates and lower by 8.9% from last year. The decrease in spending was primarily due to a sharp decline in improvement (remodeling) spending, which declined 13.0%. Over the year, remodeling spending was down 18.0%. Both spending on single-family and multifamily construction were unchanged from August but were down by 2.4% and 0.2% from a year ago, respectively. The decline in single-family construction spending is consistent with weak builder sentiment reflected in the NAHB/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index (HMI) , amid rising interest rates, energy and material costs. The NAHB construction spending index shown in the graph below illustrates how spending on single-family construction has slowed since early 2024, reflecting the impacts of elevated interest rates and ongoing uncertainty over building material tariffs. Multifamily construction spending growth has also slowed down after the peak in June 2023, with the index largely plateauing since late 2024. In contrast, improvement spending has been on an upward trend since 2023, supported in part by the aging housing stock and sustained demand for renovation . However, the latest data is consistent with a 2026 soft patch for remodeling. Private nonresidential construction spending continued its upward trend. September’s spending rose 1.1% to a SAAR of $790.6 billion, and is 2.3% higher compared to the previous year. Data center construction, a subcategory within office cons truction , remained strong with spending increasing 8.6% month-over-month and 90.3% year-over-year, due to buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure. items.title: October Jobs Report: Surging Payrolls and Hiring Uptick Means Fed Hawks Can Exhale
items.description: October Jobs Report: Surging Payrolls and Hiring Uptick Means Fed Hawks Can Exhale By Jake Krimmel Nov 06, 2026 October Payrolls Jump 165,000, More Than Double Expectations, With 84,000 Jobs Revised Up Today’s October jobs report was impressive. Coming in, we would have been happy with the forecasted 65,000, more than double last month’s. Instead we got more than double those expectations, with payrolls up 165,000. Revisions added another 84,000 jobs to August and September, lifting the three-month average to 137,000 from about 51,000 a month ago. The unemployment rate slipped to 4.1%, just as the Chicago Fed predicted , while labor force participation rose to 61.9%, above the 61.8% expected. Both moved just a smidge, but together they are notable. Wages firmed too, up 0.4% in the month and 3.1% from a year ago, versus 3.0% in September. This is still a low hire, low fire market overall, but we could be seeing some green shoots on the hiring side. The numbers could still be revised, of course, and the trend matters more than any one point; but you don’t get a good trend without a good month. A Strong Report Clears the Way for the Fed’s Next Hike For the Fed, this clears the way for a hike. After last month’s hot inflation print put the next increase in ‘when’ not ‘if’ territory, a soft jobs report was the one thing that could have complicated December. If Fed hawks were waiting to exhale, they can do so now. CME FedWatch saw Fed hike odds increase, as anticipated. The 10-year yield edged up on the announcement, and yields and hike odds remain the two things to watch for mortgage rates. Midterms or Not, Housing Needs Real Wage Gains and Cooler Inflation One question that keeps coming up is whether the midterms changed anything for the housing market. In the short run, not much – the Iran War and its impact on inflation and mortgage rates remain the major wildcard. Getting back to “normal” in many metros takes more activity, which depends on improved buying power to bring buyers off the sidelines. Mortgage rates have declined for three straight weeks, to 7.18% , after a massive 74 basis point surge from late August to mid-October, but wages are the other half of buying power. That 3.1% annual wage growth is nominal, and it trails September’s 3.7% inflation and likely won’t keep up with where inflation is headed. Nominal wage growth is necessary but not sufficient for real wage gains in this environment, so inflation has to come back down too. A more dynamic labor market and cooling inflation are sorely needed for demand.

items.title: Mortgage Applications Decline as Higher Rates Boost ARM Share
items.description: Mortgage Applications Decline as Higher Rates Boost ARM Share November 4, 2026 Catherine Koh No Comments Mortgage application activity declined in October as the 30-year fixed mortgage rate rose sharply again . The Mortgage Bankers Association’s (MBA) Market Composite Index, a measure of total mortgage application volume, fell 14.1% month-over-month in October on a seasonally adjusted basis. Compared to a year ago, total mortgage applications were 39.8% lower. Higher fixed mortgage rates continued to drive borrowers toward adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs), whose share of total applications increased to 10.8%. Steep declines occurred in both major components as the average contract rate for a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage jumped 35 basis points (bps) to an average of 7.4% in October. Purchase applications decreased 11.9% from September, while refinance applications declined 17.3%. Relative to October 2025, purchase and refinance activity were also down 17.3% and 58.5%, respectively. Meanwhile, the average contract interest rate for 5/1 ARMs was 6.4% in October. The lower initial interest rate and monthly payments made ARMs relatively more attractive to borrowers, contributing to a 0.7% increase month-over-month. Nonetheless, ARMs remained 31.1% lower than a year ago. The ARMs share of total applications for October increased 1.5 percentage points to 10.8%. Meanwhile, applications for fixed-rate mortgages declined 15.5% month-over-month and 40.7% year-over-year. Average loan sizes declined across most categories in October. The overall loan size decreased 1.5% to $375,200. Purchase loans, however, saw a marginal increase of 0.5% to an average loan size of $448,500. Meanwhile, the average refinance loan size declined 8.0% to $257,840, and ARMs loan size declined 4.8% to an average of $854,180. items.title: October Job Growth Beats Expectations, Keeping a December Fed Hike on the Table
items.description: October Job Growth Beats Expectations, Keeping a December Fed Hike on the Table Published on November 6th, 2026 by Chen Zhao Takeaway: A strong jobs report gives the Fed permission to hike again in December should they want to. This morning’s data shows that 165,000 jobs were created in October and 84,000 more jobs were created in August and September than previously reported. That brings the six-month moving average of job creation to 83,000 jobs per month after briefly dipping into negative territory last fall. The professional and business services sector saw outsized gains with 70,000 jobs created in October, the strongest month in four years. If this doesn’t get revised away in coming months, it would be a significant data point to counter AI-related labor market anxiety. The unemployment rate ticked down very slightly by 0.03 pp to 4.14%. It had gotten as high as 4.5% last November before gradually drifting down. At this point, despite all the wild month-to-month swings after the BLS updated their methodology, it’s pretty clear the labor market strengthened meaningfully as the year went on. In recent months, the Fed has not been making their policy decisions based on the jobs report because they’re more worried about the inflation side of their mandate than unemployment. Today’s data allows them to continue that stance. Regarding the December 9th meeting, a hike is already mostly priced in. There’s still next Tuesday’s inflation data and one more jobs report before the meeting, but given the recent commentary from officials, a hike seems pretty likely. Chen Zhao Chen Zhao is the head of economics research, where she produces research on the housing market for public and internal audiences. Previously, she was an executive director leading housing finance and financial markets research at the JPMorgan Chase Institute. Prior to joining JPMCI, Chen was an economics consultant at Analysis Group, Inc., where she worked on financial litigation cases and led teams conducting health economics and outcomes research on behalf of pharmaceutical companies. items.title: Homebuyers Get Some Relief as Prices Decline For Third Straight Week, Monthly Payments Dip
items.description: Homebuyers Get Some Relief as Prices Decline For Third Straight Week, Monthly Payments Dip Published on November 5th, 2026 by Dana Anderson New listings of homes for sale fell to their lowest level since the start of the year, but there are still significantly more sellers than buyers in the market. What to know about the U.S. housing market for the four weeks ending November 1: Prices fell for the third week in a row. The median home-sale price was $388,604, down 0.4% year over year. That marks the third straight week in which prices declined after three years of increases. Monthly payments dropped to a 5-week low. The median monthly mortgage payment was $2,777, down from a peak of $2,811 in early October. This data is seasonally adjusted. Costs declined because mortgage rates and sale prices are slowly coming down. House hunting activity declined. Pending home sales fell 0.6% week over week to the lowest level in records dating back to 2021. Sellers pulled back, too. New listings dropped 1.5% from a week earlier to the lowest level since January, as would-be sellers reacted to slow demand. The slow market is giving buyers room to negotiate. The buyers who are out there may be able to negotiate prices down and/or get other concessions from sellers. Buyers have more homes to choose from than a year ago, and less competition: There are 2.1% more homes on the market than a year ago, while homes are taking a bit longer to sell. items.title: Interior Finishes: The Most Time-Consuming Stage of Single-family Construction
items.description: Interior Finishes: The Most Time-Consuming Stage of Single-family Construction November 2, 2026 Paul Emrath No Comments Interior finishes (drywall, interior doors, painting, cabinets, countertops, plumbing fixtures, flooring, etc.) take more time to complete—6.4 weeks, on average—than any other major stage of single-family construction, according to results from the latest NAHB/Well Fargo Housing Market Index (HMI) survey. The October 2026 HMI survey asked builders how long it takes to complete each of the seven major stages of construction traditionally used in NAHB’s construction cost surveys . The survey covers the steps a builder typically takes after purchasing a finished lot in the leading case of a single-family detached home built for sale . After interior finishes, framing and major systems rough-ins (HVAC and plumbing/electrical other than fixtures) consume the most time: 3.7 weeks each. Final steps (landscaping, outdoor structures and clean-up) require 3.6 weeks, and exterior finishes (siding, roofing, windows & doors) require 3.4. The earliest stages of the construction process, site work and foundations, require the least amount of time—a little over two weeks each, on average. The most time-consuming stages of construction are also in general the costliest. In NAHB’s latest construction cost survey, for example, interior finishes account for over 24% of the builder’s construction costs, significantly more than any other stage of construction and roughly proportional to the amount of time that stage consumes in the overall construction process. Final steps, however, break this general rule by being the least expensive stage of construction but consuming a disproportionately large amount of construction time. The complete cost breakdown by stage of construction, along with a more detailed description of each stage, is available in Cost of Constructing a Home-2024 . In total, NAHB’s October 2026 HMI survey shows that it takes 25.3 weeks (about 5.8 months) to build the average single-family detached home, close to the average time of 6.1 months from start to completion reported by the Census Bureau for a single-family home built for sale in 2025. The Census estimates show that custom homes (e.g., contractor-built homes built one at a time on the home owner’s lot, and owner-built homes where the owner functions as the general contractor) take significantly more time to complete. Moreover, these numbers are averages, and it’s important to remember that the time it takes to build a particular home will vary based on geography and characteristics of the home and its builder. The Census Bureau’s time-to-completion estimate is based on a considerably larger and more intricately stratified sample than the one from NAHB. Hence, the Census estimate is the one you would use if you’re interested simply in total construction time for a single-family home. NAHB’s new 25.3-week time-to-completion estimate, however, has the obvious advantage of breaking down the time by stage of construction. The extra detail may be useful to a builder who wants to educate customers, decide when to purchase building materials, schedule inspections, or manage subcontractors. construction time , Housing Market Index (HMI) Prev Previous Student Housing Construction Rises in the Third Quarter Next Private Residential Construction Slips as Remodeling Weakens Next Leave a Reply Cancel reply Your email address will not be published. items.title: Zillow's agent tie-ins grab purchase share as market shrinks
items.description: Zillow's agent tie-ins grab purchase share as market shrinks By Brad Finkelstein CloseText About Brad twitter nmnbrad mailto bradley.finkelstein@arizent.com linkedin brad-finkelstein-8b2b9a5/ Published November 05, 2026, 4:39 p.m. EST | Updated November 05, 2026, 4:45 p.m. EST 3 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Zillow's strategy of pairing its loan officers with invitation-only real estate agents is pulling purchase business away from the rest of the market. Its home loans unit grew purchase volume 55% in the third quarter while industry purchase originations fell. Processing Content Zillow Home Loans originated $1.972 billion of purchase loans in the third quarter, up from $1.276 billion a year earlier. Year-to-date volume is up 79%. Over the same quarter, Zillow estimates industry purchase origination volume declined 4%. "It's why purchase mortgage revenue for us is outgrowing the category even with the category declining," said CEO Jeremy Wacksman on the earnings call. The company is almost entirely a purchase lender. It did just $4 million of refinance production in the third quarter, versus $5 million one year prior. Second quarter volume was $2.181 billion, with only $7 million coming from refi. How the Preferred program feeds Zillow Home Loans The volume growth came as Zillow expanded the share of buyer connections sent through its Preferred program, an invitation-only network of real estate agents. Zillow previously called the program Flex. Executives reported double-digit adoption of Zillow Home Loans among customers working with Preferred agents. In Zillow's oldest markets, that rate is approximately 20%. "We are pleased that we continue to see double-digit customer adoption rates in Zillow Home Loans with our oldest markets at approximately 20% adoption rates, demonstrating that our integrated experience is adding value for both consumers and real estate agents," said Jeremy Hoffman, chief operating and chief financial officer. Wacksman framed the integrated model as the reason for Zillow's confidence in mortgage growth. "I mean 80% of buyers need both the mortgage and the agent. They want that as a one-stop shop," he said. "When we can offer that as an integrated experience, that's what they're choosing." He added that "a key part of this strategy is making sure that the Home Loans loan officer and the Preferred agent build a mutually beneficial relationship." The shift also changes how Zillow gets paid. Under its legacy advertising model, real estate agents used co-marketing dollars from lenders when bidding on leads, said Douglas Harter of BTIG. Under the Preferred model, Zillow captures mortgage revenue at origination, which can come six to 12 months later. Why mortgage revenue still missed The volume gains did not translate into the revenue analysts expected. Mortgage revenue rose 32% year-over-year to $70 million, but Keefe, Bruyette & Woods had forecast $81.3 million, putting the result 13.9% short. BTIG had forecast $81 million. Hoffman attributed the miss to " rate shock , which caused lower conversions." Industry purchase volume also came in weaker than Zillow planned for. "We estimate that industry mortgage purchase origination volumes were down 4% for Q3, below our expectation for a low-single-digit decline," he said. "We call out mortgage industry performance because the majority of Zillow buyers purchased their home with a mortgage." Harter tied the broader earnings miss to a weakening housing market and the "accelerated transition from the legacy ad model to Flex." Zillow underperformed existing home sales for the first time since the fourth quarter of 2024, which helped spread the miss into mortgage, he said in a research note. Zillow posted a $158 million net loss for the quarter, compared with $10 million of net income in the third quarter of 2025. Zillow expects a steeper purchase decline in Q4 Zillow guided fourth quarter mortgage revenue to between $55 million and $56 million, with total revenue between $635 million and $665 million. "Our revenue outlook includes our expectation for a decline in year-over-year mortgage industry purchase origination volumes of 10% to 15%," Hoffman said. "This is down significantly from our prior industry expectation of mid-single-digits decline due to the sharp increase in mortgage rates we saw at the end of Q3 and into the start of Q4." Zillow expects 20% revenue growth in the fourth quarter as it scales outside its residential business, "with mortgage tailing off," Harter said. "The weakening housing market and bigger-than-anticipated model transition impact contributed to an 8-9% reduction in the 4Q revenue guide from the prior implied level," he said. "Headwinds are expected to carry into '27." Brad Finkelstein Originations Editor Brad Finkelstein is the originations editor of National Mortgage News. items.title: HELOC originations up 20%: Lead with equity as refis stall
items.description: HELOC originations up 20%: Lead with equity as refis stall By Colin McNamara Published November 05, 2026, 10:20 a.m. EST | Updated November 05, 2026, 11:01 a.m. EST 2 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Expert Quote: "Home equity demand should remain relatively resilient, supported by several quarters of steady HELOC growth." — Satyan Merchant, Senior Vice President, TransUnion Supporting Data: HELOCs accounted for more than half of all home equity activity in the second quarter. Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. As interest rates remain elevated , borrowers are searching for solutions that unlock home equity without requiring a mortgage refinance. Processing Content Home equity originations increased 10.1% year over year to 757,000 in the second quarter, with home equity line of credit originations rising 20.3%, according to TransUnion's Q3 2026 Credit Industry Insights Report. HELOCs accounted for more than half of all home equity activity. "Homeowners are increasingly turning to home equity products as a way to access cash without giving up the low rates on their primary mortgage," Satyan Merchant, senior vice president, automotive and mortgage business leader at TransUnion, told National Mortgage News. "Demand is likely to remain strongest for HELOCs, which offer flexible, on-demand access to equity while preserving existing first-lien financing." Satyan Merchant, senior vice president, automotive and mortgage business leader at TransUnion Mortgage originations as a whole jumped 12.8% on an annual basis to 1.5 million in the second quarter, as lower rates supported stronger activity. Refinance volume rose about 40%, increasing its share of total originations to 21.5% from 17.4% a year earlier. Rate-and-term refinances led the spike, jumping nearly 60%, according to the report. But interest rates rose above last year's levels for much of the third quarter and all of the fourth quarter so far, which Merchant expects to sideline homebuyers and subdue activity. The 30-year fixed rate mortgage has fallen recently, down to 7.24% last week, but it remains more than a percentage point above the same week last year, according to Freddie Mac. "However, home equity demand should remain relatively resilient, supported by several quarters of steady HELOC growth as homeowners continue to tap accumulated equity rather than refinance into higher-rate mortgages," Merchant added. Finance of America's third quarter earnings further portrayed this. The reverse mortgage lender's funded volume increased 24% year over year and 2% from the second quarter while the rest of the industry struggled to combat high rates. Mortgage performance was generally stable, although serious delinquency rates continued to normalize from historically low pandemic-era levels. The percentage of borrowers 60 or more days delinquent reached 1.64% in the third quarter. The increases concentrated primarily among Federal Housing Administration loans, which now represent nearly half of all seriously delinquent mortgage accounts. Performance on other loan types, including Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and jumbo, were steady. "Looking ahead, interest rates will continue to shape purchase and refinance demand," Merchant said. "At the same time, home equity products may remain an important source of liquidity for borrowers seeking to preserve their low mortgage rates." items.description: Gain on sale margins to slip in 2027, analysts warn By Brad Finkelstein CloseText About Brad twitter nmnbrad mailto bradley.finkelstein@arizent.com linkedin brad-finkelstein-8b2b9a5/ Published November 02, 2026, 2:35 p.m. EST 5 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Key Insight: The reason analysts cut Rocket's estimates stems from management's own downbeat internal projections. What's at Stake: PennyMac's path to a double-digit return on equity as macroeconomic headwinds mount. Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. While Rocket's third quarter earnings beat analyst estimates, the dire industry forecast management gave has led a pair of stock analysts to drop their forward estimates on the company. Meanwhile, at PennyMac Financial Services, which also released results on Thursday, it too saw the earnings outlook lowered, plus Keefe, Bruyette & Woods downgraded its stock. Processing Content On the earnings call, Rocket management said its own internal data is showing origination volume for the fourth quarter and in 2027 performing worse than what the Mortgage Bankers Association and Fannie Mae economists have forecast. Management also adjusted Rocket's guidance, although as the KBW report from Bose George noted, the fourth quarter outlook assumes continued market share gains. In the third quarter Rocket grew purchase by 0.3 percentage points to 6.5%, while refinance increased to 15.5% versus 14.3% in the second quarter. KBW's reasons for changing Rocket's forecast "[Rocket's] Management reiterated confidence in its longer-term targets of 8% purchase and 20% refinance share," George said. "We estimate purchase and refinance share of 7.1% and 15.4%, respectively, for full-year 2027, leaving potential upside if the combined platform delivers faster gains than we currently assume." This led George to drop his full year earnings per share estimate for 2026 by 2 cents to 56 cents per share. But he made larger cuts over the next two years. For 2027, the new estimate is also 56 cents per share, but this compares with the previous 70 cents per share. He dropped 2028 EPS to 74 cents per share from 90 cents. BTIG's analysts also adjusted the earnings forecast at Rocket for this year and next, noting the "more challenging" mortgage market. What BTIG sees happening with Rocket Rocket's third quarter results and its guidance for the current period "exhibited both the relative strength and the limitations from a challenging mortgage environment; we think both factors are likely to continue over the near-term," said Douglas Harter of BTIG. "The lack of visibility into meaningful improvement in earnings power means the shares appear fairly valued and the quality of the franchise/level of execution limit the downside." Harter cut the 2026 EPS forecast at Rocket by 1 cent, to 55 cents per share. For next year, the estimate was dropped by 3 cents, to 62 cents per share. But Harter left his 2028 estimate at 76 cents per share. BTIG also decreased its origination volume estimates by 4%, 11% and 3% in 2026 through 2028 respectively, "given the persistence of higher mortgage rates," the report said. What the analysts see for Rocket's volume For this year, Rocket will end up with $172.8 billion of originations, but this is expected to fall to $156.8 billion in 2027, BTIG said. In 2025, Rocket did $130.4 billion; but it acquired Redfin at the beginning of the third quarter that year, and Mr. Cooper at the start of the fourth , which were not included in its prior results. Also in February, Rocket/Redfin entered into a marketing partnership with Compass. Combining with Mr. Cooper gave Rocket the industry's largest servicing portfolio and management keyed on the recapture potential it brings. KBW is forecasting $173.6 billion this year, with $168 billion in 2027 and $200 billion the following year. In his report, George said he expects 2027 volume of $1.86 trillion, "well below normalized levels, suggesting earnings upside over time as activity recovers." The target price was reduced to $16 per share from $17 by KBW. Harter dropped the gain on sale revenue forecast by 5% lower this year and 9% lower in 2027 as a result. "This decline is partially offset by lower expenses as we expect Rocket to continue to reduce expenses in a lower volume environment," Harter said. KBW expects Rocket to report gain on sale across all of its channels of 262 basis points for the full year. For both 2027 and 2028, George foresees 255 basis points each year. items.title: Alliance's Industrial Strength Draws Huge Spec Development From Trammell Crow And PGIM
items.description: A joint venture of two commercial real estate powerhouses just broke ground on a massive speculative project in one of Dallas-Fort Worth’s hottest industrial submarkets. A rendering of the next phase of the Eagle 35 logistics hub in Fort Worth Trammell Crow Co . and joint venture partner PGIM , the investment management arm of Prudential Financial , started work on a nearly 756K SF industrial park in the AllianceTexas area of Fort Worth. The three-building development is the fourth phase of the joint venture’s 35 Eagle logistics hub . ”Dallas-Fort Worth is one of the nation’s most resilient industrial markets, supported by strong demand for modern logistics facilities,” PGIM Real Estate Head of U.S. Equity Soultana Reigle said in a statement. “We see significant opportunity in partnering with TCC to advance this development, meet the evolving needs of today’s industrial users and capitalize on the region’s long-term growth fundamentals.” DFW's industrial leasing total of 22.7M SF during the third quarter nearly matched the region's record total of 23M SF set in Q2 2021, according to the latest data from Cushman & Wakefield . The Alliance area was by far the most popular industrial destination in North Texas, absorbing more than 3.6M SF during the quarter. During the first nine months of the year, Alliance absorbed more than 7.6M SF, double the total of the next-closest submarket in DFW. Alliance’s year-to-date totals of more than 10M SF of leasing activity and 5M SF of deliveries are all also tops in the region. The industrial project from Trammell Crow and PGIM will also add to the submarket’s DFW-leading 8.3M SF under construction. The buildings are being built on 58 acres at the northwest corner of Interstate 35 West and Eagle Parkway. Fifth Third Bank and American National Bank provided construction financing for the project. Alliance Architects is the project’s architect, FCL Builders is the general contractor, and Halff is the civil engineer. The 1.4M SF mall was built in 2002 and renovated after a ferocious 2017 hailstorm that seriously damaged the property and led to its temporary closure. It was 98% occupied as of Aug. 31, according to the SEC filing. The mall added Cavender’s Boot City as a new tenant earlier this month. In early 2025, Colorado Mills was reappraised at $135M, 37% less than its 2014 valuation. Simon took out a $117.7M loan in 2014 that was transferred to special servicing before its November 2024 maturity date, Bisnow previously reported . In May 2025, after the property was reappraised, Simon avoided default on the loan by securing a two-year extension deal . Colorado Mills’ net operating income has fluctuated over the years, but the property appears to be performing better this year. Its net operating income through the first seven months of 2026 was about $18.7M, up nearly $1.3M from last year, according to the SEC filing. Colorado Mills’ $80M CMBS loan is part of an $805M pool with 63 commercial mortgage loans backed by 79 properties across the U.S. The local mall’s loan is the largest in the pool, accounting for about 10%, Kroll Bond Rating Agency said in a statement. Malls across the country have faced shifting market conditions over the past decade. The number of malls in the U.S. dropped from 2,500 in the 1980s to 700 in 2024. Despite the closures, malls are now the “top performer in commercial real estate,” with values increasing 13% year-over-year, The Wall Street Journal reported . Park Meadows mall in Lone Tree also faced a potential default in 2024. The mall’s owner, Brookfield Properties, refinanced by securing a $700M loan with a five-year term just days before its previous $615M property loan matured. items.title: Q3 multifamily sales jumped 139% on Vivmark deal
items.description: Q3 multifamily sales jumped 139% on Vivmark deal Although the mega-merger made 2026’s third quarter the highest on record, apartment values fell 4.6% year over year and 6.2% at an annualized rate between Q2 and Q3. Published Nov. 2, 2026 Leslie Shaver Senior Reporter Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google The Avalon at Palisades in Charlotte, North Carolina. AvalonBay Communities acquired the property before it became Vivmark. Permission granted by AvalonBay Communities Dive Brief: The third-quarter apartment sales landscape was very similar to August’s, with sluggish single-asset sales. Still, the merger of Equity Residential and AvalonBay Communities drove deal volume up 139% year over year to $114.1 billion, according to a report that data firm MSCI Real Assets shared with Multifamily Dive. The RCA CPPI for apartments declined 4.6% YOY. It fell 6.2% at an annualized rate between Q2 and Q3, as pricing deteriorated over the past four months. The annualized decline in values in each quarter has outpaced the yearly drop. In contrast, the RCA US National All-Property CPP rose 0.9% YOY. Without the creation of Vivmark, sales would have fallen 7% YOY for the quarter and been flat so far for the first nine months of the year. However, with the deal, 2026’s third quarter was the largest on record, surpassing $90.4 billion in 2021 and $78.4 billion in 2022. It was the second-largest quarter on record, falling only behind Q4 2021, which tallied $167.1 billion in trades. Dive Insight: Prices usually follow transaction growth, with investors underwriting appreciation as they bid, according to MSCI. “Here, volume is rising while prices fall, which points to a single transaction rather than broader confidence in the apartment sector,” MSCI said in the report. The usual gauge of industry health, individual sales, dropped 12% YOY to $34.3 billion in Q3, marking the second straight quarter of decline. In the six major metros, individual sales were approximately flat at $11.8 billion, while they dropped 17% YOY to $22.5 billion in non-major cities. The Vivmark deal pushed up volume across various subtypes. Portfolio sales rose 19% YOY to $10.2 billion on the strength of the Vivmark deal, while mid- and high-rise transactions jumped 248% YOY to $70.2 billion. The market was hardly thriving before the 10-year Treasury began rising six months ago. But since then volumes have declined, and cap rates have risen. In Q1 2022, cap rates sat at 4.5%, according to MSCI’s hedonic rate calculation. Now they’re 140 basis points higher. While much of that movement came in early 2024, they climbed 20 bps over the last year to 5.9% in Q3. As the 10-year Treasury moved above 5% in Q3, owners say it has become difficult to project deals they’re underwriting . “The last 60 days have been difficult, and from our end makes it difficult to pin down where we think exit caps are going,” American South Capital Partners Executive Vice President Tyler Epps told Multifamily Dive. Tyler Chesser, the co-founder and managing partner of CF Capital, said that “cap rates have moved out since the September [Federal Reserve] meeting,” and sellers are slow to accept it. “Historically it takes a few quarters for seller expectations to catch up to the market,” Chesser previously told Multifamily Dive. “Until they do, the bid-ask gap means a lot of deals stall, get retraded, or die.” Click here to sign up to receive multifamily and apartment news like this article in your inbox every weekday. items.title: Banks are turning cautious on lending, according to the Fed. What it means for the economy
items.description: Small businesses feel the squeeze Commercial and industrial lending to large and middle-market firms was broadly unchanged from the previous survey — but banks tightened lending to smaller businesses. "Banks reported tightening standards for premiums charged on riskier loans for firms of all sizes," the report noted. Lenders pointed to a less favorable or more uncertain economic outlook, and a worsening of industry-specific problems as the key reason for the shift. U.S. 10-Year Treasurys. Commercial real estate is also emerging as a pressure point, with banks reporting tightened standards across the board on construction and land development, nonfarm nonresidential properties, and multifamily properties, and weakening demand for loans in all CRE categories. U.S. banks are also tightening credit standards for nonbank financial firms such as private equity funds and business and mortgage credit intermediaries. The pullback comes amid growing demand for liquidity from private equity funds and business credit intermediaries, with lenders again highlighting prevailing economic uncertainty and concerns over the deteriorating financial strength among NDFI borrowers. Household credit turns selective Meanwhile, household credit sentiment appears mixed. While banks have left mortgage standards broadly unchanged, there has been some easing for jumbo mortgages — but tighter rules for subprime loans — as banks reported weaker demand, on balance, across all residential real estate loan categories. "Banks reported being more likely to approve credit card applications to super-prime and prime borrowers and less likely to approve applications to subprime borrowers, with small banks driving the trend for subprime borrowers," the report added. watch now VIDEO 6:32 06:32 Citi’s Andy Sieg weighs in on whether cracks are forming in private credit Halftime Report The squeeze comes as borrowing costs moved sharply higher during the third quarter. The 10-year Treasury note yield — the main benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — hit an intraday high of 5.349% on Oct. 5, its highest level since April 2002, amid concerns over rising U.S. debt. Tiffany Wilding, managing director and economist at PIMCO, said small businesses, housing and debt-laden firms face tighter credit and higher borrowing costs as the AI investment boom squeezes other parts of the U.S. economy. "Higher government bond yields have catalyzed a broader repricing of credit risk, especially for lower-quality borrowers," Wilding said in a note Oct. 28. Signals of credit stress among riskier households chime with a recent CNBC and SurveyMonkey poll , which found that one in five Americans who rent or have a mortgage spend at least half of their pretax income on housing, while 49% spend between 25% and 49%. Lender guidance recommends consumers spend 28% to 30% of their income on housing. A separate Federal Reserve report indicated that U.S. families' ability to address their debts has worsened over the past three years. The Fed's latest Survey of Consumer Finances, released Oct. 9, found that the percentage of families behind on loan payments at the end of 2025 reached almost 20%, up from about 12% in the previous survey in 2022.
